question: ap1
title: Acute AP-1 degradation after a priming pulse
description: Induce a transient stimulus, then rapidly degrade FOS or JUN with an inducible degron (e.g., dTAG or auxin-inducible) at defined times after washout. Track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), enhancer marks (H3K27ac), and expression of putative memory genes over days; persistence after AP-1 loss would support a self-sustaining memory, while rapid decay would argue AP-1 is only a transient readout.

question: ap1
title: Time-course of chromatin persistence at AP-1 sites with motif-mutant controls
description: After a single pulse with washout, profile CUT&RUN for AP-1 and ATAC-seq/H3K4me1/H3K27ac at multiple timepoints out to weeks. Compare enhancers with intact AP-1 motifs against CRISPR-edited motif-mutant versions of the same elements to test whether AP-1 binding is required for the persistent chromatin state.

question: ap1
title: Priming-and-reinduction assay for transcriptional memory
description: Prime cells with a sub-threshold stimulus, wait variable intervals, then re-stimulate and measure the speed and magnitude of FOS/JUN induction and downstream target expression relative to naive cells. Repeat in cells carrying AP-1 binding-site mutations or lacking a chromatin-remodeling cofactor to see whether faster or stronger reinduction depends on AP-1 itself.

question: ap1
title: Live reporter lineage tracing of AP-1 activity across divisions
description: Use a destabilized-fluorescent AP-1 target reporter combined with a stable lineage barcode or histone-label to follow individual cells through several divisions after stimulation. Sort subpopulations by heritable reporter state and compare their chromatin landscapes and response to a second stimulus, testing whether AP-1 activity states are inherited through cell division.

question: ap1
title: Stabilized AP-1 variant sufficiency and ensemble reactivation test
description: Express a degradation-resistant or long-lived AP-1 isoform (e.g., a ΔFosB-like stabilized FOS) and test whether it extends the duration of induced chromatin and behavioral or functional changes beyond wild-type lifetimes. Pair this with activity-dependent ensemble tagging and optogenetic or chemogenetic reactivation to determine whether reactivating the tagged, AP-1-positive population is necessary and sufficient to recall the stored state.

question: ap1
title: Acute AP-1 degradation after a stimulus pulse
description: Use a degron-tagged FOS or JUN allele (e.g., dTAG or auxin-inducible) to degrade AP-1 at defined times after a single stimulus. If AP-1 is the memory mechanism, the later response to restimulation should be lost or reduced when AP-1 is removed during the rest period, but not when it is removed before the first stimulus.

question: ap1
title: Time-course of chromatin persistence after AP-1 occupancy is lost
description: After a stimulus pulse, run ATAC-seq, H3K27ac/H3K4me1 CUT&RUN, and FOS/JUN CUT&RUN at several time points during washout. A memory mechanism predicts that enhancers keep open or primed chromatin after AP-1 leaves them, and that this persistence depends on the AP-1 motifs and on the stimulus having occurred.

question: ap1
title: Motif-mutation test of recall at endogenous memory loci
description: Use CRISPR base editing or prime editing to mutate AP-1 motifs at enhancers of genes that show a primed, faster response on restimulation. Compare the stimulus-recall response (fold induction and kinetics) of mutant and wild-type cells in a rested-then-restimulated paradigm to test whether the motifs are required for memory.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell tracking of AP-1 history through divisions
description: Combine a live AP-1 activity reporter (for example, a destabilized fluorescent protein under an AP-1-responsive or Fos promoter) with lineage barcodes and single-cell multiome readout. Compare cells with different prior AP-1 histories to see whether the prior state is inherited by daughter cells and predicts their later response, which separates a heritable memory from stochastic cell-to-cell variation.

question: ap1
title: Engram-style necessity test in vivo
description: In a mouse model such as hippocampal engram or tissue-resident immune memory, label cells active during a learning or priming event with an activity-dependent tag (for example, a Fos-based TRAP system). Then use time-restricted dominant-negative or conditional Fos/Jun inhibition during consolidation or recall, and measure whether the memory-dependent reactivation and the tagged cells' chromatin state are disrupted.

question: ap1
title: Post-stimulus washout time-course of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin
description: After a defined AP-1-inducing stimulus, track c-Jun/c-Fos/ATF3 occupancy (CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and transcription (RNA-seq) at many time points after withdrawal. Memory is supported if AP-1 binding and enhancer opening persist after transcripts return to baseline, and the persistence window is quantified per locus.

question: ap1
title: Inducible AP-1 degradation during distinct phases of the memory window
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron or dTAG system on Fos or Jun to deplete AP-1 at different times: during priming, during the quiescent interval, and at re-stimulation. If memory is AP-1-dependent, depletion during the maintenance phase should abolish the enhanced or faster re-induction of memory genes, while depletion only during priming should have a different effect.

question: ap1
title: Motif and enhancer perturbation with sufficiency tests
description: Use base editing or CRISPR deletion to mutate AP-1 motifs within enhancers that carry the memory signature, and measure whether priming-dependent faster or stronger re-induction is lost while the first response is preserved. Complement this with dCas9-tethered c-Jun, Fos, or p300 at silent sites to test whether AP-1 recruitment alone is sufficient to install a memory-like state.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 memory heritability
description: Combine a live AP-1 transcriptional reporter with lineage barcoding, then pulse stimulate and follow cells over several divisions without further stimulus. Measure whether daughter cells inherit the primed state and its re-inducibility, and whether the memory is a stable cell-intrinsic state or a population-level drift that dissipates.

question: ap1
title: In vivo tagging and recall challenge of stimulus-experienced cells
description: Label cells that experienced an AP-1-inducing stimulus in vivo using a Fos-based activity tag such as Fos-CreER or TRAP, then challenge the animal or transplant the tagged cells and measure the recall response. Test necessity by ablating or AP-1-depleting the tagged population and checking whether the enhanced recall response disappears, which would connect the molecular memory to a functional outcome.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-resolved, time-stamped AP-1 reporter tracing
description: Build an inducible, lineage-tracing system (e.g., a Cre- or Dre-recombinase reporter driven by AP-1-responsive enhancers) that permanently marks cells that experienced a transient AP-1 pulse, then wash out the stimulus and track whether marked cells retain altered chromatin or transcription after days to weeks. Persistence in marked cells after the stimulus is removed, without ongoing AP-1 activity, would be direct evidence of memory.

question: ap1
title: Acute AP-1 degradation or inhibition during the memory window
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron (or a dominant-negative c-Jun/Fos or a photo-controllable AP-1 inhibitor) to remove AP-1 at defined times: during the stimulus, after the stimulus, and during re-stimulation. If AP-1 is a true memory mechanism, the altered chromatin state or primed gene response should persist when AP-1 is removed after induction, but be lost when AP-1 is removed during the initial pulse or the reactivation step.

question: ap1
title: Chromatin persistence profiling (ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN, H3K27ac) across a stimulus-washout time course
description: Profile AP-1 occupancy (c-Fos/c-Jun CUT&RUN) together with chromatin accessibility and histone marks at multiple timepoints after a transient stimulus and after a second stimulus. Testing whether enhancers that were bound by AP-1 during the pulse remain open or marked after AP-1 leaves the chromatin distinguishes genuine epigenetic memory from simple ongoing transcription.

question: ap1
title: Re-stimulation kinetics and priming assays
description: Compare the transcriptional and AP-1 binding response to a second identical stimulus in naive versus previously stimulated cells, measuring the speed, amplitude, and gene set of the response (e.g., by time-resolved RNA-seq or live single-cell reporters). Faster or stronger re-induction of the same target genes in primed cells, and dependence of that priming on the original AP-1 pulse, would support a memory function rather than a simple dose response.

question: ap1
title: Mechanistic dissection of the memory determinants with targeted perturbations
description: Combine targeted epigenome editing (dCas9-based writers/erasers such as p300 or LSD1 fused to AP-1-bound loci) with mutations in the AP-1 binding motifs and in putative self-reinforcing partners (e.g., BAF complex, bromodomain proteins) to test which features are necessary and sufficient for persistence. Showing that a chromatin mark at a single AP-1-bound enhancer can by itself reproduce or abolish the memory effect would establish a causal mechanism rather than correlation.

question: ap1
title: Washout and re-challenge hysteresis assay
description: Pulse cells with a stimulus, withdraw it, and track AP-1 target gene expression over time. Memory would appear as persistent expression after withdrawal and faster or stronger re-induction on re-challenge, which should be lost in AP-1 mutants lacking DNA binding or dimerization.

question: ap1
title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the rest phase
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron on FOS or JUN to remove AP-1 after priming but before re-challenge. If AP-1 is the memory substrate, degradation should erase the primed state, while degradation before priming should prevent it from forming.

question: ap1
title: Chromatin persistence time course (ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN, H3K27ac)
description: Profile AP-1 occupancy and enhancer accessibility and acetylation at primed and naive sites across a stimulus-withdrawal time course. This tests whether chromatin opening outlasts AP-1 binding and whether it is maintained by AP-1 itself or by a separate epigenetic mechanism.

question: ap1
title: Live single-cell reporter with lineage tracking
description: Express a fluorescent AP-1 target reporter, prime cells, and follow individual lineages through several divisions by time-lapse imaging. Quantify how long the primed state persists and whether it is inherited by daughter cells, and test whether mitotic bookmarking or chromatin-remodeling perturbations shorten that inheritance.

question: ap1
title: Feedback-loop perturbation and bistability testing
description: Disrupt candidate positive feedback loops (FOS autoregulation, ATF3 or JUN loops) and co-activator inhibition (p300/CBP or BRD4) in single-cell reporter lines. Memory should scale with loop strength and show bimodal, cell-autonomous persistence rather than a population-average decay, and this should be validated in vivo with a repeated-stimulus model.

question: ap1
title: Stimulus washout with chromatin and re-stimulation time course
description: After a defined AP-1-inducing stimulus, wash it out and track FOS/JUN occupancy (CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and enhancer marks (H3K27ac) over days. Then re-stimulate and compare the speed and magnitude of target gene induction against naive cells, since faster or stronger re-induction without new AP-1 binding would indicate a memory.

question: ap1
title: Inducible degradation of AP-1 during and after a priming window
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-degradable FOS or JUN allele to remove AP-1 at different times relative to a priming stimulus. Measure whether the memory-like transcriptional and chromatin state persists after AP-1 is gone, which separates AP-1 being required to establish memory from being required to maintain it.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic tethered AP-1 memory circuit at a reporter locus
description: Tether engineered AP-1 components (or a dimerized bZIP fusion) to a single-copy reporter with a dox-controlled recruiter, then turn the recruiter off and measure reporter expression, chromatin state, and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 over weeks. Persistence without the tether would show that AP-1 is sufficient to write a self-maintaining state, while mutating its DNA-binding domain would test necessity.

question: ap1
title: Live single-cell AP-1 reporter tracking across repeated pulses
description: Track AP-1 activity in individual cells with a live fluorescent reporter during repeated stimulus pulses of varying spacing and strength. Test whether prior pulse history predicts later response magnitude or timing (for example with mutual information or Markov models), and whether this history-dependence is lost when cells are imaged in heterogeneous or lineage-tracked populations.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-chase protein turnover versus persistence of memory
description: Use SNAP- or HaloTag-labelled FOS/JUN with pulse-chase labelling to measure AP-1 protein and DNA-bound half-lives in the same cells where memory persists. If memory lasts well beyond AP-1 turnover, combined with mutation of AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers (base editing) and Micro-C or Hi-C for 3D contacts, this would point toward an epigenetic or 3D-architecture-based mechanism rather than a self-sustaining AP-1 feedback loop.

question: ap1
title: Stimulus washout with persistence tracking
description: Induce AP-1 activity with a controlled stimulus or an inducible Fos/Jun system, then withdraw it and track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and target-gene expression over days. Memory is supported if these marks and transcripts stay elevated after AP-1 activity returns to baseline, and decay kinetics can be compared with control sites.

question: ap1
title: Rechallenge test for primed responses
description: Compare first and second exposures to the same stimulus after a rest period, measuring the speed, amplitude, and AP-1 target-gene induction in each. Repeating this in Fos or Jun knockout and dominant-negative cells tests whether AP-1 is required for the faster, stronger secondary response.

question: ap1
title: Causal dissection of AP-1 motifs at memory enhancers
description: Identify enhancers that stay open after washout, then use CRISPR base editing or saturation mutagenesis to disrupt their AP-1 motifs. Check whether accessibility persistence and faster re-induction are lost, and use dCas9-based epigenetic editing to test whether AP-1 binding alone is sufficient to restore the memory signal.

question: ap1
title: Mapping AP-1 occupancy versus epigenetic retention over time
description: Run CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for c-Fos and c-Jun alongside histone marks across a stimulation and washout time course. This shows whether memory is carried by retained histone marks after AP-1 has left the chromatin (bookmarking), or whether AP-1 must rebind at each re-exposure.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell live reporting of activation history across divisions
description: Use a destabilized fluorescent reporter driven by the Fos promoter, with live imaging and lineage tracking, to record each cell's prior activation history. Test whether past AP-1 activity predicts future response in the same cell and whether that history is inherited by daughter cells, which would distinguish cell-intrinsic memory from population-level effects.

question: ap1
title: Inducible, time-resolved AP-1 perturbation with chromatin-memory readout
description: Use an acute, reversible degron (e.g., dTAG or AID) or optogenetic control to deplete or activate FOS/JUN for defined windows, then track whether chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac and AP-1 motif occupancy at enhancers persist after the stimulus is withdrawn. Persistence of these marks without AP-1 present would be direct evidence of memory, while rapid collapse would argue against it.

question: ap1
title: Stimulus re-exposure (memory recall) assay
description: Apply a priming stimulus (e.g., a short TNF or growth-factor pulse), allow a rest period, then re-stimulate and compare the magnitude and kinetics of AP-1 target gene induction (RNA-seq, nascent transcription via PRO-seq) with naive cells. Faster or stronger responses on re-challenge, lost when AP-1 binding sites are mutated or AP-1 is degraded during the rest period, would demonstrate a functional memory.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 activity history
description: Combine a live AP-1 reporter (e.g., FOS-promoter-driven fluorescent timer or destabilized reporter) with barcoded lineage tracing or CRISPR-based recorders to link each cell's past AP-1 activity to its later transcriptional state after a delay. Correlating prior pulse history with future responses across single-cell clones tests whether history is stored and inherited rather than just reflecting current state.

question: ap1
title: Site-specific mutagenesis of AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or prime editing to mutate individual TRE/AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers and measure, in the same cells, the effect on the persistence of chromatin opening and on the re-induction kinetics after a washout. Mutations that abolish memory while leaving the initial response intact would separate the storage function from the acute transcriptional function.

question: ap1
title: Biochemical test of self-sustaining AP-1 chromatin states and dilution
description: Track histone marks and AP-1/co-factor occupancy through cell division using pulse-chase labeling (e.g., SNAP-tag or Hdac/histone turnover reporters) and CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq with and without DNA replication. If AP-1 binding and the associated marks are re-established by sister chromatids or through inheritance of modified histones, that supports a self-propagating mechanism, whereas dilution after division indicates memory requires continuous AP-1 presence.

question: ap1
title: Flip-flop test with inducible AP-1 switch (electronics latch analogy)
description: Borrowing from an SR latch in electronics, which holds its state after the input pulse ends, use an optogenetic or degron-based system to pulse AP-1 (e.g., Fos/Jun) activity briefly, then withdraw it and track ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for AP-1 and H3K27ac, and target-gene transcription over days. Memory is supported only if the chromatin and transcriptional state persist without ongoing AP-1 input, and the persistence should disappear when AP-1 binding sites are mutated.

question: ap1
title: Savings paradigm: faster re-induction after rest (relearning-curve analogy)
description: Following Ebbinghaus-style savings experiments in psychology, stimulate cells with a first exposure, rest them, then re-stimulate and compare the speed, amplitude, and magnitude of AP-1 target induction (time-resolved RNA-seq or live Fos/Jun reporters) against naive cells. A savings effect that vanishes in cells lacking AP-1 or with binding-site mutations would support a memory role specifically for AP-1.

question: ap1
title: Dendrochronology-style recorder for past AP-1 activity
description: Like tree rings that record past growing seasons, use a stable recorder such as an inducible CreER or a slow-maturing fluorescent timer under an AP-1 responsive promoter to permanently mark cells that had AP-1 activity at a defined time. Then measure, by flow or imaging, whether marked cells respond differently to a later stimulus and whether the mark is retained across divisions and after AP-1 withdrawal.

question: ap1
title: Serial-passage propagation test (sourdough starter analogy)
description: A sourdough starter keeps its character only by being transferred serially, so test whether AP-1-induced states are carried forward the same way: stimulate a culture, then passage cells through many divisions without stimulus, sampling at intervals for chromatin accessibility and transcription at AP-1 targets. Persistence across passages, measured against lineage-matched controls and AP-1 knockouts, would indicate heritable memory rather than a transient response.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic bookmarking dissection with degron-based AP-1 removal
description: Drawing on the idea of a bookmark that survives a page turn, synchronize cells, remove AP-1 specifically in mitosis or G1 using a degron, and measure whether AP-1-bound enhancers keep accessibility and H3K27ac through mitosis and into daughter cells. Comparing retention with versus without AP-1 binding and with dCas9 site-specific mutants would separate active memory maintenance from passive chromatin persistence.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis loop test of path dependence (physics)
description: Borrowing from ferromagnetic hysteresis, sweep stimulus strength up and then back down while measuring phospho-Jun/Fos levels and AP-1 target accessibility (ATAC or CUT&RUN) at each step. Memory is supported if the descending branch stays elevated relative to the ascending one, with loop area scaling with prior exposure and abolished by an AP-1 dominant-negative.

question: ap1
title: Seed bank dormancy and reactivation (ecology)
description: Analogous to dormant seeds that germinate after variable dormancy, prime cells, then rest them for different durations before re-stimulation. Use a degron-tagged or inducible Fos/Jun to remove AP-1 either during the rest period or only at recall; if memory is AP-1-dependent, faster reactivation should require AP-1 to persist through rest, and its loss during rest should erase the advantage.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-chase age dating of AP-1-bound sites (geochronology)
description: Like dating strata by isotope decay, tag endogenous Fos or Jun with a HaloTag or SNAP tag, label it with a dye during a priming pulse, and chase for increasing times. Measuring which AP-1-occupied enhancers still carry the old label reveals whether a long-lived, distinct subset of sites constitutes the memory, versus transient occupancy that turns over.

question: ap1
title: Retroactive interference paradigm (experimental psychology)
description: Following classic interference designs from memory research, prime cells with an AP-1-driving stimulus, then expose them to an unrelated or competing stimulus set before testing recall. A true AP-1 memory should show specific decay with interference strength and its retention should be predicted by the magnitude of AP-1 target occupancy measured right after priming.

question: ap1
title: Heritable lineage recorder across divisions (molecular recording / bookkeeping)
description: Analogous to a ledger that carries balances forward, build an AP-1-responsive recorder (e.g., a Cre or CRISPR-scar reporter, or a timer fluorophore) to log past activity, then sort daughter cells after several divisions and challenge them. Memory is cell-intrinsic and inherited if the recorded history predicts the progeny's recall response, independent of population-level selection, which can be checked with clonal barcoding.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis loop of AP-1 occupancy (magnetism analogy)
description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., phorbol ester or growth factor dose) up and then back down, and measure AP-1 genomic occupancy (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN) and target-gene output at matched doses on each branch. A memory mechanism predicts a hysteresis loop, where the ascending and descending curves diverge at the same stimulus level, while a purely reactive system retraces the same path.

question: ap1
title: Anamnestic recall test with a degron-based memory eraser (immunological memory analogy)
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, let them rest, then restimulate, comparing primary and secondary AP-1 target-gene induction kinetics and chromatin opening. Using a dTAG or auxin degron on JUN or FOS applied only during the rest interval, a true memory should be lost (secondary response reverts to primary), separating the role of persistent AP-1 from its acute activity.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-chase half-life of AP-1 binding (radioactive decay analogy)
description: Pulse-label endogenous JUN/FOS with a HaloTag or SNAP-tag and track the fraction of tagged protein and of chromatin-bound AP-1 after a stimulus is withdrawn, fitting decay curves at individual enhancers. Comparing the half-life of bound complexes with the half-life of the transcript and protein reveals whether AP-1 occupancy outlasts its trigger on a timescale long enough to count as memory.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic bistable toggle with an AP-1 feedback loop (electronic flip-flop analogy)
description: Build a synthetic circuit in which an inducible FOS/JUN cassette drives its own expression through AP-1 sites and reads out a fluorescent reporter, then test whether a brief inducer pulse produces a persistent ON state after the inducer is removed. Varying the strength of the positive feedback and the AP-1 site number maps the conditions required for bistability, which is a necessary property of a memory element.

question: ap1
title: Lineage recording of past AP-1 activity (cell-tape recorder analogy)
description: Use an AP-1-responsive promoter to drive a CRISPR-based or base-editing recorder that writes irreversible barcode mutations into a tape locus whenever AP-1 is active. Then track the recorded cells by single-cell lineage and transcriptomics, asking whether cells with a prior AP-1 record show altered responses to a later, unrelated stimulus relative to unrecorded sister cells, which tests whether past AP-1 activity causally shapes future behavior.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis loop test (magnetism analogy)
description: In magnetic materials, memory is shown by history-dependent response: the output on re-application of a field depends on the previous field sweep. Apply pulsed AP-1 stimuli (e.g., TPA or growth factor) with varied pulse number, spacing, and amplitude, then measure a second, identical stimulus and quantify the hysteresis of target gene expression and chromatin accessibility at AP-1 enhancers. Memory is supported if the response to the second pulse depends on the first pulse's history beyond what the current AP-1 level predicts.

question: ap1
title: Seed-bank dormancy and reactivation (ecology analogy)
description: Seeds persist in a dormant state and germinate faster after a prior cue. Use an acute, degron-based FOS or JUN depletion to end AP-1 signaling after a stimulus, then track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN), enhancer accessibility (ATAC-seq), and target transcription over days. Memory predicts that enhancers stay primed after AP-1 protein is gone and that a later sub-threshold stimulus reactivates them faster than in naive cells.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic flip-flop circuit (electronics analogy)
description: A flip-flop stores one bit because its outputs feed back to hold the state after the input pulse ends. Build an engineered AP-1 positive-feedback loop, with an AP-1-responsive promoter driving a FOS or JUN transgene, and test bistability using transient inducer pulses and a flow-cytometry readout. Breaking the loop (mutating the AP-1 sites in the feedback element or using a non-feedback control) should abolish the stored state, which would show that the self-reinforcing loop, not the pulse itself, is the memory element.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-barcoded memory transmission (immunological recall analogy)
description: Immune memory is clonal: cells that saw an antigen divide and pass on a faster, stronger secondary response. Combine lineage barcoding with a live AP-1 activity reporter, sort cells by prior exposure history, and use single-cell multiome to track whether AP-1-primed chromatin states are inherited through mitosis and show faster re-induction in daughter clones. Memory requires that the primed state is heritable across divisions, not just re-established by each new stimulus.

question: ap1
title: Dated stratigraphic layering (sediment core analogy)
description: Sediment cores record events as dated layers, so the time of deposition can be read from depth. Use sequential pulse-chase labeling of AP-1 components with orthogonal tags (e.g., HaloTag or SNAP-tag pulses at successive time points) and map which enhancers retain each labeled AP-1 layer, using CUT&Tag and ATAC-seq. Layers that persist after the tag signal has cleared, and that are not explained by dilution through cell division, would indicate durable, time-stamped AP-1 memory at specific loci.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis test with degron-controlled AP-1 washout
description: Borrowing from magnetic hysteresis, apply graded AP-1 stimulation doses, then rapidly deplete c-Fos or JunB with an auxin-inducible degron and track enhancer accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and target-gene transcription over days. Memory is supported if the chromatin and expression state persists after AP-1 is gone, and the persistence scales with prior dose, unlike a transient response that returns to baseline.

question: ap1
title: Shape-memory 'training' by repeated stimulation cycles
description: Like shape-memory alloys that recover faster after thermal training, expose cells to repeated AP-1-inducing pulses at varying inter-pulse intervals and compare second-round kinetics with naive cells. Live single-cell AP-1 reporters (e.g., FosB-driven or ATF3 reporters) would show whether priming produces faster, stronger, or more sustained re-activation, and whether the effect depends on the interval length.

question: ap1
title: Stratigraphic timestamping of AP-1 binding events
description: Using the logic of sedimentary layers read in order of deposition, pair a time-resolved tag (e.g., a tamoxifen-inducible or photoconvertible reporter, or pulse-labeled histone marks) with AP-1 ChIP/CUT&RUN at successive time points to see which enhancers were occupied during each stimulation 'layer.' Sites that retain an early-layer tag after AP-1 has left would constitute a durable molecular record of past activity.

question: ap1
title: Capture-recapture of stimulated cells
description: Adapting mark-recapture estimation from ecology, irreversibly label cells that experienced an AP-1 pulse (e.g., via a Cre/Tamoxifen-based or CaMPARI-type photoconversion marker), then later re-stimulate and measure what fraction of the marked population responds more strongly than unlabeled cells. Quantifying the retention and re-response of the marked population over time estimates how long and how reliably the memory persists per cell.

question: ap1
title: Latch versus integrator test via rescue of AP-1 after loss
description: Analogous to distinguishing a self-holding digital latch from a leaky integrator, delete AP-1 at varying times after induction and then re-express it at defined windows (or target dCas9-based recruitment of Fos/Jun to a single memory-associated locus). If the memory state is self-sustaining, re-expression will not be required to maintain it, and the locus-specific reinstatement will test whether the memory is autonomous at that enhancer.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis loop from pulse-dose-duration sweeps (physics analogy)
description: Borrowing from magnetic hysteresis, vary the dose and duration of an inducible FOS/JUN pulse, then wash out and measure chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target transcription at multiple times afterward. Memory is supported if the post-washout state depends on the path taken (a loop rather than a single curve), and it should persist past the point where AP-1 binding has returned to baseline.

question: ap1
title: Secondary-response test (immunological memory analogy)
description: As in vaccine recall, compare primary and secondary responses to identical AP-1 stimuli, measuring the speed, amplitude, and target-gene breadth of the second response in cells with and without a rest interval. Memory requires the secondary response to be faster or stronger, and this advantage should disappear when AP-1 is depleted with a degron (e.g., dTAG-FOS) during the rest period.

question: ap1
title: Volatile vs. non-volatile storage test (computer-memory analogy)
description: Distinguish 'RAM-like' from 'flash-like' storage by degrading AP-1 (dTAG or auxin system) during the quiescent interval and checking whether the primed state is retained. If the state persists without AP-1 present, the memory is stored in a self-sustaining chromatin or feedback state; if it is lost, the memory depends on continuous AP-1 activity.

question: ap1
title: Seed-bank dormancy with lineage-tracked heritability (ecology analogy)
description: Use a barcoded, live AP-1 reporter to pulse-label a cell population, then follow single-cell lineages through several divisions without stimulus, sorting cells at each generation for re-challenge. Heritable memory is shown if the primed fraction persists across divisions and re-challenge response is enriched in descendants, analogous to a seed bank that keeps viable seeds across generations.

question: ap1
title: Stratigraphic dating of AP-1 occupancy (geology analogy)
description: Like dating sediment layers, use HaloTag or SNAP-tag pulse-chase on endogenous FOS/JUN to timestamp when each AP-1 binding event was made, then ChIP-seq at several chase times to build a layered record of occupancy. Persistent 'layers' of marks that outlast the tagged protein at their sites would indicate an epigenetic memory, while sites that clear with the protein would indicate transient binding.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis loop test (materials science analogy)
description: Ramp FOS/JUN levels up and down with an inducible degron (e.g., AID or dTAG) or a titratable Dox system, and measure chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target transcription at each level. A true memory mechanism should show different on and off thresholds, so the loop area tracks stored state, while AP-1 motif-mutant enhancers should produce no loop.

question: ap1
title: Time-stamped activity recorder (dendrochronology analogy)
description: Use sequential, orthogonally inducible lineage tags such as Fos-CreERT2 pulses at different times to mark cells by when AP-1 was active, like growth rings. Then, after stimulus withdrawal, test whether older stamps keep elevated target expression or open chromatin, and whether that persistence scales with the duration and recency of AP-1 activity.

question: ap1
title: Anamnestic re-challenge paradigm (immunological memory analogy)
description: Prime cells with a brief AP-1 stimulus, let them rest for several days, then re-challenge and compare the speed and magnitude of target induction with naive cells. Repeat in cells carrying mutations in the AP-1 sites of the primed enhancers or lacking AP-1 binding, since a memory mechanism should specifically lose the faster secondary response when its binding sites are disrupted.

question: ap1
title: History-dependence in pulse-train system identification (control theory analogy)
description: Deliver randomized optogenetic AP-1 pulse trains with varying inter-pulse intervals and fit models of target output with and without a persistent state variable. If a memory term is needed, the response to later pulses should depend on earlier pulse timing with a decay constant that matches chromatin persistence rather than mRNA or protein half-life.

question: ap1
title: Stratigraphic occupancy-versus-mark dating (radiometric dating analogy)
description: After a stimulus, use SNAP/Halo-tagged FOS pulse-chase and sequential ChIP-seq at multiple time points to build a time-resolved record of AP-1 occupancy alongside histone marks such as H3K27ac and H3K4me1 at each enhancer. Memory predicts that enhancers keeping their marks after AP-1 dissociates are the ones that stay accessible, and acutely degrading AP-1 at a chosen time point should then test whether the marks are necessary to hold that state.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis test with graded stimulus pulses (Schmitt-trigger analogy)
description: Borrowing from electronics, where a Schmitt trigger's output depends on its recent history, apply TPA or EGF pulses of varying dose and duration, then withdraw the stimulus. Measure AP-1 target accessibility and transcription at multiple times after withdrawal, and test whether the response shows a threshold and a state that persists after the input is removed (hysteresis) rather than simply tracking the input.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-chase occupancy dating (radiometric and sediment-dating analogy)
description: Borrowing from radiometric dating, where a known isotope pulse is traced through a layered record, tag endogenous Fos or Jun with a photoconvertible or HaloTag system and label AP-1 proteins at a defined time. Then follow the labelled cohort of bound sites with CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq and compare how long AP-1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility persist relative to mRNA and protein half-lives.

question: ap1
title: Inducible AP-1 degradation to test memory without the factor (forensic evidence-persistence analogy)
description: Borrowing from forensics, where a trace can outlast the actor that left it, use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron to remove Fos and Jun after a stimulus window and then measure the enhancers they opened. Quantify whether accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and the induced transcriptional state persist without AP-1 for days, which would be the key evidence that AP-1 acts as a memory rather than a continuous driver.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic AP-1 feedback circuit as a write-read-erase memory cell (ferroelectric or flash memory analogy)
description: Borrowing from non-volatile memory engineering, build a synthetic reporter in which AP-1 binding sites drive an AP-1 or Fos expression cassette, forming a self-reinforcing loop. Write a bit with a transient input, read it out a reporter, and erase it by CRISPRi or dCas9 silencing of the loop. A stable, switchable state that tracks the write and erase steps would support AP-1 feedback as a memory mechanism.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-barcoded single-cell tracking of heritable AP-1 memory (seed-bank and clonal inheritance analogy)
description: Borrowing from seed-bank ecology, where dormant propagules carry a state across generations, combine lentiviral lineage barcodes with single-cell multiome (RNA plus ATAC) after a transient AP-1-inducing stimulus. Then measure whether the stimulus-primed chromatin state and faster or stronger AP-1 target re-induction are inherited by daughter clones across several divisions and whether the memory is heterogeneous across lineages.

question: ap1
title: Stop-and-wait re-stimulation (memory dip test)
description: Apply a sustained AP-1 stimulus (e.g., inducible c-Fos/c-Jun or a defined growth factor pulse), hold it at an intermediate 'stop' for varying wait times, then withdraw and re-apply the stimulus while measuring the AP-1 target response (reporter luciferase, qPCR of targets). If AP-1 stores a memory, the re-stimulated response should show a wait-time-dependent signature that reappears when the stop is repeated, analogous to the spin-glass memory dip reappearing after re-cooling.

question: ap1
title: Stop versus no-stop control to separate memory from aging
description: Run matched-duration protocols in which the same total AP-1 exposure is delivered either continuously or interrupted by rests, and include sham-rest controls with equal elapsed time but no stimulus. Any history-dependent difference that persists beyond what time alone (aging) produces is the candidate memory signal.

question: ap1
title: Thermoremanent-style persistence readout over long timescales
description: After removing the AP-1 stimulus, measure the retained state at many later times (hours to weeks) using AP-1 occupancy (ChIP-qPCR or CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and enhancer marks at AP-1 target loci, and fit the decay of this residual signal. Persistence well beyond the transcript and protein half-lives would indicate a stored state rather than simple carryover.

question: ap1
title: Frequency-domain (ac-style) probing of AP-1 response
description: Drive AP-1 with small periodic pulses across a range of frequencies in naive versus previously stimulated cells, and measure the amplitude and phase lag of a live-cell reporter (e.g., a FRET or luciferase AP-1 sensor). A history-dependent change in the slow relaxation component, absent in naive cells, would indicate an internal memory state that the fast pulses cannot erase.

question: ap1
title: Genetic dissection with AP-1 component perturbation
description: Repeat the stop-and-wait and thermoremanent-style protocols in cells with inducible dominant-negative c-Jun (TAM67), c-Fos or JunB knockdown, and in cells lacking specific AP-1 partners, rescuing with wild-type constructs. If the memory signature disappears specifically when AP-1 function is lost and returns on rescue, AP-1 is necessary for the memory rather than just correlated with it.

question: ap1
title: Training-rest-retest protocol with a response-threshold readout
description: Borrowing the shape-memory training cycle, apply repeated AP-1-inducing pulses (e.g., TPA or EGF) with defined rest periods, then measure the dose-response or activation threshold of an AP-1 reporter on re-exposure. A lasting shift in threshold or faster re-induction (savings) after rest, compared with naive cells, would indicate a stored state rather than residual signal.

question: ap1
title: Dilatometry-style tracking of output after washout
description: Track AP-1 reporter activity and target mRNA/protein continuously through stimulus withdrawal, as dilatometry tracks strain after unloading. Fit the decay of the output and check whether a fraction persists beyond the expected half-lives of the Fos/Jun transcripts and proteins, which would point to a self-sustaining state.

question: ap1
title: Variant-identity mapping with ChIP/CUT&RUN and chromatin accessibility at memory timepoints
description: As XRD and TEM identify which martensite variants persist, map which AP-1 dimer compositions (Fos, Fra1, Jun, JunB, ATF) occupy which enhancers and what their chromatin accessibility is (ATAC-seq, H3K27ac) at multiple post-training times. Persistence of a specific occupancy and accessibility pattern at trained loci, after AP-1 protein levels return to baseline, would identify the stored microstructure.

question: ap1
title: Anneal-type dissociation test using inducible degradation
description: Analogous to annealing that erases dislocations but preserves variant arrangement, use degron-tagged or auxin-inducible Fos/Jun to clear AP-1 protein after training while leaving the epigenetic and transcript landscape intact. If the trained response is retained without AP-1 protein, the memory lies in a downstream state; if it is lost, AP-1 itself is required to hold it.

question: ap1
title: Separating memory from stress damage with dominant-negative and off-target controls
description: Mirror the test for residual stress or plastic damage by training cells with a stimulus that causes damage without engaging AP-1 (or with AP-1 blocked via TAM-67 or a dominant-negative Jun during training), then test retention. Memory that requires AP-1 engagement during training and is absent when AP-1 is blocked, while damage-matched controls show no retention, would argue for a specific AP-1-encoded state over nonspecific cellular injury.

question: ap1
title: Up-and-down stimulus ramps to map hysteresis
description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., growth factor or TPA dose) up and then back down over the same range, and measure AP-1 target output (reporter, RT-qPCR, or CUT&RUN occupancy at canonical sites) on both branches. Separated ascending and descending curves at matched stimulus levels would show that cells keep a record of their history rather than responding only to the present input.

question: ap1
title: Lag of chromatin state behind AP-1 occupancy after washout
description: Track AP-1 (Fos/Jun, via HaloTag or CUT&RUN) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) through a time course after stimulus withdrawal, analogous to checking whether adsorbate coverage lags gas-phase changes in operando spectroscopy. If accessibility and H3K27ac persist after AP-1 has left its sites, the chromatin state is retaining a record.

question: ap1
title: Priming and rest-interval re-stimulation protocol
description: Pre-condition cells with a priming pulse, then vary the rest interval before a standard re-challenge, and compare induction kinetics and magnitude with naive cells at each interval. Faster or stronger responses that decay with rest time, and that are absent in naive cells, are the signature of a stored memory of past exposure.

question: ap1
title: Degron-based removal of AP-1 during the memory window
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on Jun or Fos to remove the factor at defined times after priming, similar to a temperature-programmed desorption step that removes a species to test what is retained. If the memory phenotype survives degradation of AP-1 but is lost when the marks are erased (e.g., with a histone-acetyltransferase or chromatin-remodeler inhibitor), the memory is carried by the chromatin state rather than by the factor itself.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-tracked test of heritable persistence
description: Prime cells, then track single-cell lineages with live reporters of AP-1 activity and chromatin state through several divisions, comparing with mock-treated lineages. Persistence of the primed state across divisions without ongoing stimulation, measured against a null model of stochastic heterogeneity, would indicate a self-sustaining, heritable memory rather than transient signaling.

question: ap1
title: Washout-and-re-stimulation with protein-versus-chromatin separation
description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus (e.g., TPA or EGF), wash out, and wait variable rest intervals before re-stimulating; measure re-induction kinetics of AP-1 target genes against a naive control. To separate memory stored in AP-1 protein from memory stored in chromatin, repeat the rest period with a degron-tagged c-Fos or c-Jun so the protein is depleted while the chromatin state is retained.

question: ap1
title: Gem5-style ablation of candidate memory structures
description: Knock out or acutely degrade individual components that could hold the state, such as FOSL1, JUNB, the chromatin co-activators p300/CBP and BRD4, and the histone writers, alone and in combination. Then test which knockouts abolish the faster or stronger second response, which identifies the structure that carries the memory.

question: ap1
title: Residual-state footprinting with a history classifier
description: After stimulus washout, profile AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN) together with chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and H3K27ac at enhancers over time. Train a classifier on this residual state to predict whether a cell or population had prior stimulation; accuracy that stays above chance after the protein has cleared would show that the residual state retains the history, analogous to recovering a victim's past from predictor or cache residue.

question: ap1
title: Cross-stimulus leakage test
description: Prime cells with one AP-1-inducing stimulus, then challenge them with an unrelated stimulus that activates a non-AP-1 program, or with an AP-1 stimulus that activates a different gene set. Measure whether priming shifts the response to the new stimulus, which tests whether the memory leaks across contexts and whether it is specific to AP-1 target loci or global.

question: ap1
title: Live single-cell reporter with decay-curve fitting and binding-site mutants
description: Use a live AP-1-responsive reporter (for example, a destabilized fluorescent protein knocked into a memory-gene locus) to track single cells through stimulus, rest, and re-stimulation. Fit the decay of the memory effect against rest interval to estimate a half-life, and compare wild-type loci with AP-1 motif-mutant alleles and with a non-AP-1 stimulus matched for transcriptional output, to show that the memory depends on AP-1 binding rather than on the overall level of activation.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-withdrawal impulse-response profiling (local-projection analogue)
description: Apply a brief, calibrated AP-1 pulse (e.g., TPA, EGF, or an optogenetic c-Jun/Fos driver), then measure AP-1 target expression and chromatin accessibility at dense timepoints for days after AP-1 activity returns to baseline. Memory is supported if a later identical stimulus gives a larger or faster response than the first, and if the residual change persists after the reporter and nuclear AP-1 signal have fully decayed.

question: ap1
title: Shock size and duration grid to test scaling of the imprint
description: Cross a range of pulse amplitudes with pulse durations and quantify the residual enhancer activation or gene priming after washout for each combination. A genuine memory mechanism predicts a dose- and duration-dependent imprint with threshold or bistable behavior, whereas a simple decaying-transient model predicts the imprint vanishes in proportion to the signal.

question: ap1
title: Unit-root and persistence testing on single-cell AP-1 reporter time series
description: Track live single-cell AP-1 reporter levels (e.g., FRET or fluorescent Fos/Jun reporters) over long periods and apply unit-root and autocorrelation tests to determine whether the post-stimulus state is mean-reverting to a fixed baseline or shifts to a new stable level. A unit-root-like or multi-stable result would indicate that the cell has a stored state rather than a simple relaxation back to baseline.

question: ap1
title: Acute degron-mediated AP-1 depletion to separate imprint from ongoing signaling
description: After priming with a pulse, rapidly degrade c-Jun or Fos with an inducible degron (e.g., dTAG) at varying delays and then re-stimulate the cells. If the memory depends on AP-1 itself, the imprint should be erased by degradation at early delays and should be protected by chromatin-level marks only when the factor is removed late, which separates the AP-1-dependent component from persistence driven by ongoing dynamics or by chromatin.

question: ap1
title: Natural-experiment comparison of injury severity and exposure history in vivo
description: Use inducible lineage-traced reporters and ATAC-seq or ChIP-seq in tissues subjected to injuries of different severity and duration (e.g., skin wounding, fibrosis, or inflammatory challenge), then compare AP-1 site accessibility weeks after injury across matched cell populations with different prior exposure. Reliance on pre-existing differences, as in cross-country hysteresis studies, helps separate true AP-1-dependent memory from persistence caused by tissue repair dynamics or systemic inflammation.

question: ap1
title: Antecedent-state transfer-function model with residual diagnostics
description: Fit models that predict target-gene induction or enhancer activity from the current stimulus plus an exponentially weighted index of prior AP-1 activity, as hydrologists add antecedent wetness to rainfall-runoff models. If the antecedent term improves prediction and the residuals lose autocorrelation, that supports AP-1 carrying state forward beyond what the present stimulus explains.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis loops of AP-1 activity versus stimulus dose
description: Ramp stimulus intensity up and then back down in single-cell time series (for example, Fos or c-Jun reporter intensity against stimulus level) and compare the rising and falling limbs as sediment-concentration hysteresis is compared. A loop that persists, with a nonzero enclosed area, means the cells' AP-1 output depends on their stimulation history rather than on the current dose alone.

question: ap1
title: Paired-lineage manipulation with long-term rechallenge
description: Split genetically matched cell populations into an AP-1-perturbed arm (for example, a degron-tagged or CRISPR-disrupted Jun/Fos) and an untreated control, then give repeated stimulation cycles over weeks and compare the second-response and later-response magnitudes. The difference in memory-like priming between arms, measured against the control over many cycles, isolates AP-1's contribution.

question: ap1
title: Recession analysis of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin persistence after washout
description: After removing the stimulus, track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN or ChIP at time points) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) across hours to days, and fit exponential recession curves as hydrologists fit baseflow recession constants. Long decay constants at specific enhancers indicate stored AP-1 signal, and comparing these timescales with those of non-AP-1 transcription factors tests whether AP-1 specifically provides the storage.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-interval and antecedent-storage perturbation experiments
description: Deliver the same total AP-1 stimulation as pulses separated by different intervals, then measure re-induction after a standard challenge, and remove the putative storage (for example, by blocking AP-1 protein stability or chromatin retention) to see whether the memory effect disappears. Memory that depends on the interval and vanishes when storage is disrupted is direct evidence of an AP-1-based mechanism rather than a correlation with the current stimulus.

question: ap1
title: Stimulus-withdrawal difference-in-differences on chromatin
description: Pulse cells with an AP-1 inducer (e.g., TPA or EGF), then withdraw it. Compare the decay of ATAC-seq accessibility and H3K27ac at AP-1-bound enhancers (treated) against matched unbound control enhancers (untreated), using a DiD estimate of persistence after the trigger is gone. Persistence in treated loci but not controls would be evidence of memory rather than simple signal-following.

question: ap1
title: Survival analysis of enhancer reversion after trigger removal
description: Take dense time-course ATAC-seq or CUT&RUN after washout and model time-to-closure of each AP-1 site with a Cox or discrete-time hazard model. Covariates would include motif strength, co-bound factors such as BRD4 or p300, and the pulse dose. A memory mechanism predicts that sites with self-reinforcing features (e.g., AP-1 binding near Fos/Jun or other AP-1 target genes) have lower closure hazards.

question: ap1
title: Critical-juncture timing and counterfactual trajectory comparison
description: Deliver the same AP-1 pulse at different early windows or doses, and let each cohort evolve for days under identical conditions. Use sequence analysis on chromatin and transcriptional state trajectories, then test whether early-pulse differences produce divergent late states that a later identical challenge cannot erase. This separates history dependence from a simple read-out of current conditions.

question: ap1
title: Re-challenge test for primed responses
description: After washout, re-stimulate with a different or same signal and measure the speed and magnitude of AP-1 target induction (e.g., time to mRNA and chromatin opening) relative to naive cells, with a control for cells that never saw the pulse. Faster or stronger responses in primed cells indicate stored state. Repeat in knock-in lines with mutated AP-1 sites to test whether AP-1 binding itself is required for the primed response.

question: ap1
title: Break the self-reinforcing loop and track heritability
description: Use an inducible degron on Fos or Jun, or dCas9-based recruitment to a specific enhancer, to interrupt AP-1 autoregulation after the pulse, analogous to removing a reform's enforcement mechanism. Combine this with single-cell lineage tracing or live reporters to measure whether the memory persists across cell divisions and is lost when the feedback is broken.

question: ap1
title: Lag-dependent re-stimulation decay curves
description: Borrowing the filler-trial lag design from syntactic priming, prime cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus, then re-challenge after variable rest intervals filled with neutral or non-AP-1 stimuli. Measure the secondary induction of AP-1 target genes (RNA-seq or qPCR) and fit decay models: pure activation decay predicts exponential loss of the boost, while true memory predicts a persistent plateau that outlasts the transcription factor's own occupancy.

question: ap1
title: Dissociating AP-1 occupancy from the memory trace via inducible depletion
description: Following priming, use an auxin- or degron-inducible system to deplete c-Jun/c-Fos during the rest window, then test the secondary response. If the memory depends on ongoing AP-1 binding, depletion should abolish the boost, whereas a chromatin-based trace should survive depletion, which can be checked with ATAC-seq and H3K27ac at the same time points.

question: ap1
title: Site-specific versus generalized transfer across enhancers
description: Analogous to comparing lexically shared and non-shared prime-target pairs, test whether priming transfers to other AP-1 sites that share a motif family but not sequence context, and to sites with identical motifs in different chromatin contexts. Quantify transfer with ChIP-seq for Jun/Fos and ATAC-seq, so that item-specific (site-bound) memory can be separated from abstract, motif-level memory.

question: ap1
title: Interference from intervening non-AP-1 stimuli
description: Insert filler stimuli that activate unrelated transcription factors (e.g., NF-kB, glucocorticoid, or cAMP/CREB pathways) between priming and challenge, varying their number and strength. If the AP-1 memory is specific, its decay should depend mainly on AP-1-relevant intervening events, mirroring how filler material modulates syntactic priming decay and helping separate general activation decay from specific memory.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage tracking of memory inheritance
description: Use a live AP-1 reporter (or fluorescent Jun/Fos knock-in) combined with time-lapse imaging to track primed cells through division, then measure whether the primed state is inherited by daughter cells or reset stochastically. Fitting the distribution of responses across cells and generations can distinguish graded decay from a bistable, heritable memory state.

question: ap1
title: Epigenetic-editor sufficiency test after AP-1 removal
description: After acutely degrading JUN/FOS (for example with a dTAG system) following priming, target dCas9-p300 or dCas9-KRAB to a single primed AP-1 enhancer and test whether re-establishing its acetylation or silencing state alone reproduces or erases the memory response. This asks whether the epigenetic mark, rather than the transcription factor, is sufficient to carry the memory.

question: ap1
title: History-tagged MPRA with AP-1 motif saturation mutagenesis
description: Build a massively parallel reporter library of memory-bearing enhancers with saturation mutagenesis of AP-1 and cofactor motifs, and run each library through a prime, washout, and rechallenge design. Comparing rechallenge responses across variants identifies which sequence features are required to encode memory, separating them from features needed for the initial response.

question: ap1
title: Live imaging of AP-1 binding through mitosis with bookmarking readout
description: Use endogenous HaloTag-tagged FOS or JUN and live single-molecule or time-lapse imaging to ask which AP-1 sites remain bound on mitotic chromosomes. Then test whether daughter cells that inherit bound sites reactivate target genes faster than those that do not.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell history reporter with lineage barcodes
description: Combine a fluorescent timer or destabilized-reporter cassette under control of an AP-1 target promoter with CRISPR lineage barcodes to record each cell's past AP-1 activity. Then test whether prior activity history predicts future response within clonal lineages, after conditioning on current cell state.

question: ap1
title: Pol II pause-release kinetics at memory genes after washout
description: Use PRO-seq or NET-seq after priming and washout to measure paused RNA polymerase II and pause-release rates at memory genes, comparing primed and naive cells with and without AP-1 degradation. This tests whether the memory is held as a poised transcriptional state that is independent of persistent chromatin marks.

question: ap1
title: Single-molecule residence-time tracking of JUN/FOS after pulsed vs sustained stimulation
description: Use single-molecule tracking (HaloTag or SNAP-tagged JUN/FOS) to measure chromatin dwell times of AP-1 after a brief pulse versus continuous stimulation. If memory is encoded kinetically, cells with prolonged AP-1 dwell after a pulse should show persistent enhancer activity, and this dwell-time difference should predict the strength of later responses.

question: ap1
title: Parental-histone pulse-chase at AP-1 enhancers
description: Label pre-existing histones (e.g., SNAP-tagged H3.1/H3.3 quenched before stimulation, then pulse-labeled new histones) and track old versus new nucleosomes at AP-1 sites through stimulation, washout, and cell division. Retention of parental, modified nucleosomes at AP-1 enhancers would indicate that memory is carried by histone inheritance rather than by ongoing AP-1 occupancy.

question: ap1
title: Binding-only AP-1 tethering without transactivation domains
description: Fuse DNA-binding-competent but transactivation-deficient JUN or FOS (or a bZIP domain alone) to a synthetic recruitment system at a single reporter enhancer, then ask whether occupancy alone sustains chromatin opening after the stimulus is gone. Showing that binding is sufficient, or that activation is required, would separate AP-1 as a structural marker from AP-1 as an active memory driver.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic AP-1 site arrays at a safe-harbor locus with tunable motif affinity
description: Knock in arrays of AP-1 motifs with graded affinities and spacings at a silent safe-harbor locus, then measure which configurations generate persistent accessibility after a single stimulus. This would reveal the minimal site architecture (number, affinity, and cooperativity) required for a locus to remember an AP-1 exposure.

question: ap1
title: Phospho-degron stabilized versus wild-type FOS and JUN to decouple protein persistence from transcription
description: Generate matched FOS or JUN variants with altered phospho-degron or ubiquitin-site mutations that change protein half-life while keeping transcriptional output comparable, using pulse-chase protein measurements. If longer-lived AP-1 protein extends chromatin memory independently of transcript levels, protein persistence itself would be the memory substrate, analogous to stabilized ΔFosB.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis test with inducible AP-1 dosing
description: Ramp an inducible AP-1 (e.g., dox- or auxin-tunable Fos/Jun) up and down in a dose series, then measure the same downstream readout at a fixed final dose reached from different histories. A history-dependent (hysteretic or bistable) response that differs between up-ramp and down-ramp cells would be a direct signature of a memory state, distinct from simply asking whether AP-1 is required.

question: ap1
title: Acute degradation washout to separate protein presence from memory
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron on endogenous c-Fos or JunB to remove AP-1 protein within minutes after a priming pulse, then track a re-stimulation readout over days. If priming persists after near-complete protein loss, the memory is carried by a self-sustaining chromatin or cofactor state rather than by continued AP-1 occupancy, and proteomic or CUT&Tag profiling of the surviving state can identify the carrier.

question: ap1
title: Domain-swap test of AP-1 identity versus generic occupancy
description: Fuse the AP-1 bZIP DNA-binding domain to non-AP-1 activation domains and to unrelated activation domains with AP-1 bZIP, matching their occupancy levels at the same enhancers by ChIP and dosing. If memory tracks AP-1 identity and not just occupancy or transactivation strength, the domains that matter for persistence should be identifiable by systematic swapping.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic retention and sublineage re-induction timing
description: Use live imaging of a HaloTag-tagged JunB or Fos to measure whether AP-1 remains bound to mitotic chromosomes, and combine this with mitotic ChIP-seq. Then sort daughter-cell sublineages from a barcoded or photoconvertible lineage and measure whether the re-induction latency is inherited through division, which tests heritability of the memory state rather than its maintenance in interphase.

question: ap1
title: Time-resolved proximity labeling of AP-1 partner composition
description: Use TurboID fused to Fos or JunB and sample labeled interactomes at multiple times after a stimulus and during the quiet period. Shifts in the partner set, such as swaps between Fos, ATF3, JDP2, or cofactors, that precede or track the persistence phase would indicate a compositional switch that writes and then maintains the memory, and this can be tested by perturbing the partner that changes.

question: ap1
title: Protein-versus-chromatin dissociation with timed degron removal
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on JUN or FOS to remove AP-1 protein only during the quiescent interval after a priming pulse, then re-stimulate. If re-response is retained, memory is carried by chromatin state rather than by persisting AP-1 protein; if lost, the protein itself is required during the rest period.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic tethering of AP-1 to a neutral locus
description: Fuse a bona fide AP-1 activation domain or the bZIP domain to dCas9 or a zinc-finger array and tether it transiently to a silent reporter locus, with no endogenous signal. Measure whether chromatin opening, reporter expression, and faster re-induction persist after tether removal, which tests whether AP-1 binding alone is sufficient to write memory.

question: ap1
title: Division-coupled inheritance of memory in sorted daughter cells
description: Track HaloTag-labeled JUN or FOS with live imaging through one or more cell divisions after a priming stimulus, then sort daughter cells by nuclear AP-1 level and challenge them with re-stimulation. This tests whether memory is inherited through mitosis via bookmarking or re-established de novo by each daughter.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell information encoding of priming dose and duration
description: Vary the intensity and duration of a priming stimulus across a grid, then measure both the nuclear AP-1 dynamics during priming and the re-response in the same single cells, using barcoded or live reporters. Mutual information between priming history and re-response would quantify whether AP-1 encodes memory in its pulse features, such as amplitude, duration, or frequency.

question: ap1
title: Targeted epigenome editing at memorized AP-1 enhancers
description: Use dCas9 fused to KRAB, DNMT3A, or TET1 catalytic domains to erase or write the chromatin marks at a few individual AP-1-bound enhancers identified as memory-associated, while leaving AP-1 binding itself intact. If editing these specific enhancers abolishes or creates memory without changing AP-1 occupancy, the mark rather than the factor is the causal memory element.

question: ap1
title: Temporal necessity mapping with inducible degradation
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron knock-in on endogenous FOS or JUN to remove the protein at defined times after a priming pulse. If memory depends on AP-1 only during induction, degradation after washout should leave the primed state intact; if it depends on ongoing AP-1, the primed state should collapse at the time of degradation, which defines the length of the necessity window.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-chase turnover of endogenous AP-1 protein and its phosphorylation state
description: Tag endogenous JUN or FOS with a HaloTag or SNAP tag and perform pulse-chase labeling after stimulation, measuring protein half-life and parallel phospho-site (e.g., c-Jun S63/S73) and ubiquitination status by quantitative mass spectrometry. Comparing the decay of the protein pool with the decay of memory-gene priming tests whether a stable post-translationally modified AP-1 pool, rather than chromatin marks, carries the memory.

question: ap1
title: Saturation mutagenesis of AP-1 sites in a barcoded synthetic memory locus
description: Integrate a library of barcoded reporter constructs carrying a minimal enhancer with variable AP-1 site number, spacing, and flanking sequence into a single landing-pad locus, then pulse, wash out, and measure barcode-resolved reactivation after days. This directly tests which sequence features are sufficient to encode persistent priming, separate from the native genomic context.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic inheritance assay for AP-1-dependent memory
description: Combine a stable (long-lived) fluorescent reporter of prior AP-1 activity with lineage tracking through several cell divisions, sorting and re-challenging daughter cells by their inherited reporter state. If primed responsiveness is inherited by daughters at rates above chance and tracks reporter dilution, memory is transmitted through mitosis; if it is lost, the memory must be re-established after each division.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-frequency decoding of AP-1 memory
description: Deliver the same total stimulus dose in microfluidic chambers as a single pulse, several spaced pulses, or continuous exposure, then measure the strength and persistence of the priming signature at a fixed later time. Whether memory scales with integrated dose, the number of pulses, or the timing of the last pulse distinguishes a cumulative memory encoding from a simple last-event reporter.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic retention and clonal inheritance of AP-1 occupancy
description: Tag endogenous c-Jun with HaloTag, pulse-stimulate, then follow single cells through mitosis by live imaging and sort mitotic cells for ChIP to ask whether AP-1 stays on chromosomes at memory loci. Daughter cells that inherit the mark should respond faster on re-stimulation than sister lineages without it.

question: ap1
title: Tethered AP-1 at a silent non-enhancer locus
description: Use a dCas9 or zinc-finger tether to recruit c-Jun/Fos to a transcriptionally silent, non-AP-1 locus for a single transient pulse, then track H3K27ac and transcription for weeks. Persistence there, independent of native enhancer context, would show that AP-1 itself writes a durable state rather than just reading a pre-existing one.

question: ap1
title: Optogenetic pulse-pattern encoding of memory
description: Use light-inducible AP-1 (optoFos/optoJun) to deliver trains that vary pulse number and inter-pulse interval, then measure the magnitude of the second response. Dependence on interval rather than total dose would show that AP-1 encodes temporal history, not just its last state.

question: ap1
title: TurboID proximity labeling of cofactors that outlast AP-1
description: Fuse TurboID to AP-1 and time-resolve biotin labeling across a washout series, then use proteomics to identify co-factors that remain near memory loci after AP-1 has left. Candidates that persist without AP-1 would be the true memory carriers, and degrading them should erase the memory while leaving AP-1 intact.

question: ap1
title: Single-molecule residence time as a kinetic memory readout
description: Track single HaloTag-c-Jun molecules by live-cell single-molecule imaging before, during, and after stimulation, comparing dwell times on target enhancers. A stable change in residence time after washout, with no change in occupancy, would demonstrate kinetic memory and separate it from bulk ChIP signal.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic sufficiency test with an inducible tethered AP-1 at a silent locus
description: Tether a dimerized FOS-JUN (or bZIP fusion) to a transgenic silent reporter locus using dCas9 or a synthetic zinc-finger system under a doxycycline switch. After the tether is removed, measure whether accessibility and transcription persist, which tests whether AP-1 occupancy alone is sufficient to carry a self-sustaining memory state.

question: ap1
title: Residence-time shift of endogenous FOS/JUN by single-molecule tracking
description: Knock in HaloTag at the endogenous FOS and JUN loci and use single-molecule tracking with pulse-chase labeling to measure chromatin dwell-time distributions before, during, and after stimulation. A persistent lengthening of dwell time without changes in total occupancy would indicate that memory is encoded in binding kinetics rather than in presence or absence of the factor.

question: ap1
title: Optogenetic pulse-train encoding of AP-1 history
description: Drive a light-inducible AP-1 (e.g., optogenetic JUN or FOS) with trains that vary in pulse number, spacing, and total dose, then measure a standardized later response to a fixed challenge. If the response scales with pulse count or spacing rather than with the last pulse, AP-1 is acting as an integrator of activation history, which is a defining property of memory.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic inheritance of AP-1 priming across cell divisions
description: Track endogenously tagged AP-1 occupancy and reactivation kinetics through mitosis in live imaging, sorting or following daughter cells that inherited different amounts of bound factor. Faster or stronger reactivation in daughters that inherited high AP-1 occupancy would show that the memory is passed through cell division, distinguishing it from a purely cell-autonomous, reversible state.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-barcoded clonal tracing of primed AP-1 states
description: Combine an AP-1 activity reporter with a heritable CRISPR-based lineage barcode so each clone's history of activation is recorded. Then challenge sorted clones with a secondary stimulus and test whether clonal response biases are stable across many generations and across tissue transplantation, which would show heritable memory at the clone level.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic retention test of AP-1 at primed enhancers
description: Tag endogenous c-Jun or Fos (e.g., HaloTag) and image it through mitosis after a priming stimulus, then sort daughter cells and run ATAC-seq or CUT&Tag. If AP-1 occupancy and chromatin openness survive mitotic chromosome condensation without re-stimulation, the memory is mitotically inherited; if not, it must be re-established each cycle.

question: ap1
title: Site-specific writing and erasing of AP-1 memory with dCas9
description: Tether a dCas9-fused AP-1 subunit or a CBP/p300 activator to one defined AP-1 enhancer and, separately, dCas9-KRAB to the same site, then test whether a later stimulus response is potentiated or lost at that locus alone. This gives per-locus necessity and sufficiency without disturbing the global AP-1 pool.

question: ap1
title: Protein-turnover clock and degradation-resistant AP-1 variants
description: Measure Fos and Jun protein half-lives and phosphorylation states across the post-stimulus interval with pulse-chase labeling, to identify whether a long-lived AP-1 pool exists. Then express ubiquitin-resistant or phospho-mimetic Fos mutants that extend protein lifetime and test whether memory duration scales with protein stability rather than with transcription.

question: ap1
title: Heterodimer-identity swap to test which bZIP pairing carries memory
description: Replace Fos with ATF3, or knock in leucine-zipper chimeras that alter dimer stability and partner preference, while keeping DNA-binding fixed. Compare the persistence of accessibility and the re-stimulation response to determine whether memory depends on the specific Fos-Jun dimer composition or simply on any bZIP occupying the site.

question: ap1
title: Motif-swap specificity control at memory-bearing enhancers
description: At enhancers that show AP-1-dependent memory, replace the AP-1 motif with motifs for other stimulus-responsive factors (CREB, NFAT, ISRE, or a scrambled sequence) using CRISPR editing or MPRA-scale libraries, then measure whether the primed state persists. Memory that survives only with AP-1 motifs would support AP-1 specificity, while memory that persists with any motif would point to a generic chromatin-level mechanism.

question: ap1
title: Temporal degron window to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Use an inducible degron (auxin or dTAG) to remove Fos or Jun at different times after a stimulus pulse, then re-stimulate. If memory requires AP-1 only during establishment, late removal leaves re-induction intact; if it requires ongoing AP-1, late removal erases it.

question: ap1
title: Occupancy versus chromatin persistence time course
description: Run CUT&Tag for Fos/Jun alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac at memory-gene enhancers across a time course after pulse withdrawal. If accessibility and H3K27ac outlast AP-1 occupancy, the chromatin state, not the transcription factor, is carrying the memory.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic bookmarking and heritable memory
description: Image whether AP-1 stays on mitotic chromosomes and combine barcoded lineage tracing with a pulse to ask whether the primed state is inherited by daughter cells. Persistence through division would support a heritable, cell-intrinsic memory rather than a signal re-supplied each time.

question: ap1
title: Heterodimer composition swap knock-ins
description: Replace c-Jun with JunB, or Fos with Fra1 or ATF3, at the endogenous locus and compare the strength and duration of memory after a pulse. If memory depends on partner identity rather than total AP-1 activity, specific dimer composition, not just presence, encodes the memory.

question: ap1
title: Locus-specific synthetic recruitment and hysteresis
description: Pulse a tethered AP-1 fragment, or a dimerizer-recruited Jun, onto a silent reporter and release it, then monitor whether the reporter stays active. Combining this with dose ramps up and down tests whether AP-1 alone can produce a stable, hysteretic switch at a locus.

question: ap1
title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the post-stimulus window
description: Use dTAG or auxin-inducible degradation of Fos or Jun after an initial stimulus, then re-stimulate. If the second response and chromatin priming fail when AP-1 is removed during washout, AP-1 is necessary for memory maintenance rather than only for initial induction.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-interval series to measure memory decay kinetics
description: Deliver two stimulus pulses separated by systematically varied intervals, using optogenetic or precisely timed ligand pulses, and measure the second response (transcription, AP-1 binding, accessibility). The interval-dependence curve gives a quantitative memory timescale that can be compared against models of simple signal carryover.

question: ap1
title: Motif-level editing of AP-1 sites at memory enhancers
description: Use base editing or CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at enhancers that gain accessibility or activity after stimulation, leaving neighboring sequence intact.
