Measuring whether the motif loss abolishes priming and faster re-induction tests whether the AP-1 site itself, rather than the bound factor or general chromatin state, encodes memory.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic inheritance of AP-1-primed chromatin
description: Synchronize cells, stimulate, and track AP-1 occupancy and accessibility through mitosis into daughter cells, combining mitotic ChIP or CUT&Tag with clonal readouts. Retention of the primed state across division would indicate heritable memory, whereas loss would indicate that memory depends on continuous AP-1 presence.

question: ap1
title: Barcoded single-cell lineage tracing of memory heterogeneity
description: Introduce lineage barcodes and a fluorescent AP-1 target reporter, then stimulate cells and follow clonal lineages over several divisions. Comparing memory between sister and unrelated clones reveals whether memory is cell-autonomous, inherited, and bistable or whether it is a graded, population-level effect.

question: ap1
title: Washout-and-rechallenge chromatin persistence
description: After a defined AP-1-inducing stimulus is removed, track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) and accessibility (ATAC-seq) at target enhancers over days, then re-stimulate. Memory is supported if persistent AP-1 binding predicts faster or stronger secondary transcription, and fails if binding decays first.

question: ap1
title: Degron-timed necessity test
description: Use AID or dTAG to deplete c-Fos or JunB in defined windows: during the initial stimulus, and only during the post-stimulus washout period. Comparing re-challenge responses shows whether AP-1 is required to write the memory or only to execute the first response.

question: ap1
title: Tether-and-release sufficiency test
description: Use inducible dCas9 fused to Fos-Jun or ATF3 at a minimal enhancer, then remove the tether. If accessibility and transcription persist without the original stimulus, AP-1 binding itself is sufficient to hold a chromatin state, which is the core claim of a memory mechanism.

question: ap1
title: Memory across cell division
description: Track AP-1 occupancy on mitotic chromosomes (live imaging or mitotic ChIP) and measure whether a secondary response in daughter cells depends on the parent's prior stimulation. This tests whether AP-1 provides mitotic bookmarking that could carry memory through proliferation.

question: ap1
title: Stimulus-history encoding with a live reporter
description: Vary the timing, duration, and frequency of stimuli while imaging a live AP-1-responsive reporter in single cells. Hysteresis or history-dependent thresholds that match a fitted bistable model would show AP-1 encodes past input, rather than just reporting the current signal.

question: ap1
title: Washout time course with paired ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN
description: After a defined AP-1-inducing stimulus, withdraw it and profile AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for Fos/JunB) alongside chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) at multiple time points. Memory is supported if accessibility and faster re-induction persist at sites where AP-1 has left, and the persistence rate separates it from simple binding.

question: ap1
title: Degron-based necessity test after priming
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on Fos or Jun, degrading the protein only after the priming window closes and before re-stimulation. If the primed response is lost, AP-1 is required to maintain memory; if it persists, AP-1 only establishes the state.

question: ap1
title: dCas9-AP-1 tethering for sufficiency, then tether removal
description: Tether Jun or Fos to a normally silent locus with dCas9 to test whether AP-1 alone can establish a primed state. Then remove the tether and track whether the locus stays accessible and responsive on re-stimulation, which would indicate self-sustaining memory.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic bookmarking and inheritance by daughter cells
description: Profile AP-1 and chromatin accessibility in mitotically arrested cells and combine live imaging of fluorescent AP-1 reporters with division tracking. This tests whether AP-1 binding or the primed state is inherited through mitosis, a key criterion for a cellular memory mechanism.

question: ap1
title: Lineage recording of past AP-1 activity linked to single-cell state
description: Use a Fos-driven recorder (such as FosTRAP) to label cells by their prior AP-1 activity, then run single-cell multiome on the labeled and unlabeled populations after re-stimulation. This links the history of AP-1 activity to later chromatin and transcriptional variability within the same tissue.

question: ap1
title: Degron timing to separate maintenance from establishment
description: Add an auxin-inducible degron to endogenous Fos and JunB, then deplete AP-1 at varying times after a priming pulse. If the primed response or chromatin state is lost only when AP-1 is removed during the memory window, AP-1 is required to maintain the memory rather than only to set it up.

question: ap1
title: Protein turnover versus chromatin residence
description: Use Halo or SNAP tags on Fos or Jun to measure protein half-life and chromatin dwell time by pulse-chase. If the chromatin mark outlasts the protein, memory must be carried by something other than AP-1 protein itself, such as a self-sustaining chromatin state.

question: ap1
title: Motif-level necessity at endogenous enhancers
description: Use base or prime editing to mutate AP-1 motifs in endogenous enhancers, then track accessibility and H3K27ac through a stimulus-washout time course. Retained chromatin opening that depends on the intact motif is a direct test of AP-1 as the memory element.

question: ap1
title: Heritability of the primed state through division
description: Use live single-cell reporters with barcoded lineage tracking to ask whether the primed state passes to daughter cells. Combine this with AP-1 perturbation to see whether heritability depends on AP-1 itself.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-history and re-stimulation kinetics
description: Vary the number, spacing and interval of AP-1 inducing pulses, then measure how fast and how strongly cells respond on re-stimulation. This shows whether AP-1 encodes input history in a way that matches training-like memory, and it can be fitted to a model.

question: ap1
title: Acute AP-1 depletion after washout
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron (e.g., AID2) to remove FOS or JUN after the stimulus is withdrawn and measure whether target gene expression and chromatin states persist. If memory collapses on depletion, AP-1 is required to maintain it rather than just to write it.

question: ap1
title: Enhancer motif mutants tested for chromatin memory
description: CRISPR-mutate AP-1 motifs in candidate memory enhancers, then run ATAC-seq and H3K27ac time courses after washout in wild-type and mutant cells. Loss of persistence at mutant enhancers would show that AP-1 binding is required for chromatin-level memory.

question: ap1
title: Pulsed optogenetic training with hysteresis readout
description: Drive AP-1 with light pulses that vary in frequency, number, and spacing, then measure gene expression and the speed and magnitude of re-induction after a rest period. This tests whether the system encodes stimulus history and how the encoding depends on pulse pattern.

question: ap1
title: Barcoded lineage tracing of memory across divisions
description: Pair AP-1-responsive reporters with heritable barcodes and track single-cell memory states across many generations. Tracking whether the primed state is passed to daughters, and at what fidelity, distinguishes heritable memory from memory that is re-established each cycle.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic AP-1 feedback circuit for bistability
description: Build an AP-1 autoregulatory loop in a controlled cell line and test whether it sustains expression after the inducer is removed, and whether it shows bistable switching. This checks whether AP-1 self-reinforcement is sufficient for memory, independent of native chromatin context.

question: ap1
title: Degron-mediated AP-1 depletion after priming
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, then acutely degrade Fos or Jun (dTAG or auxin system) during the quiescent window. If AP-1 is required to maintain memory, accessibility and re-induction should collapse; if not, memory is self-sustaining after AP-1 leaves the chromatin.

question: ap1
title: Single-molecule footprinting of AP-1 occupancy in the quiescent phase
description: Use single-molecule footprinting on memory enhancers after washout to measure what fraction of alleles still carry AP-1 and how long footprints persist. Distinguishing continuous occupancy from re-binding of a fresh pool directly tests whether the memory is held by persistent AP-1 binding.

question: ap1
title: Motif deletion or base editing at memory enhancers
description: Use CRISPR deletion or base editing to disrupt AP-1 motifs at enhancers that retain accessibility after priming, then measure retained accessibility, H3K27ac, and the speed and magnitude of re-induction. This tests necessity at the sequence level rather than relying on correlation.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic inheritance of AP-1 memory
description: Tag endogenous Fos or Jun and image it through mitosis, while tracking accessibility or reporter output in daughter cells. Persistence of AP-1 on mitotic chromatin and matched inherited memory would support a heritable, bookmarking-based mechanism.

question: ap1
title: dCas9-tethered AP-1 sufficiency test at silent loci
description: Tether c-Jun or a p300-recruiting AP-1 fragment to silent loci with dCas9, then wash out and measure whether the locus keeps an open, primed state and responds faster on re-stimulation. This tests whether AP-1 recruitment alone can install memory, independent of upstream signaling.

question: ap1
title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, then rapidly degrade c-Fos or c-Jun using a dTAG or AID system and test whether the primed transcriptional response on a second stimulus is lost. If the memory survives degradation, AP-1 is not required to store it; if it disappears, AP-1 itself is the memory carrier.

question: ap1
title: Chromatin persistence time-course after washout
description: Run ATAC-seq and H3K27ac CUT&Tag at many time points after stimulus removal to measure how long AP-1-bound enhancers stay open and active. Pair this with CRISPR mutation of AP-1 motifs at those enhancers to test whether persistence depends on AP-1 binding.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic inheritance of AP-1 memory
description: Use live imaging of Fos/Jun reporters through mitosis, and sort daughter cells after division to measure whether AP-1 occupancy and enhancer accessibility are passed to them. Retention across division would support a mitotic bookmarking mechanism for memory.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-pattern encoding with optogenetic AP-1
description: Drive AP-1 activity with optogenetic pulses that vary in frequency, duration, and number, then measure how each pattern changes the response to a later test stimulus. This tests whether memory depends on the history of AP-1 dynamics rather than on a single active state.

question: ap1
title: Barcoded lineage tracing of past AP-1 activity
description: Label cells by their AP-1 activity history with a heritable reporter and barcode them, then profile the population later to see whether past AP-1 activity predicts present transcriptional state. This tests memory at the level of individual cells across time and division.

question: ap1
title: Washout-and-rechallenge time course (tests persistence)
description: Pulse cells with the stimulus for defined durations and doses, wash out, then rechallenge at multiple rest intervals (hours to weeks). Track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for JUN/FOS), chromatin accessibility, and the speed and amplitude of target-gene re-induction. Memory is supported only if rechallenge responses persist beyond the decay of the acute signal, and they should scale with pulse dose and duration.

question: ap1
title: Acute degron during the rest window (tests causal necessity)
description: Tag endogenous JUN and/or FOS with an auxin-inducible degron (or use a rapid optogenetic/chemical degradation system) and degrade AP-1 specifically during the quiescent interval between stimulus and rechallenge. If rechallenge response is lost while chromatin accessibility is preserved, AP-1 protein is required for maintenance; if it is retained, AP-1 is only a re-initiator.

question: ap1
title: Paralog-resolved dissection and dimer-swap rescue (tests unit assumption)
description: Perform CUT&RUN and rechallenge assays for each AP-1 family member separately (JUN, JUNB, FOS, FOSL1, ATF3) and knock out individual members to find which ones carry the memory. Then perform dimer-swap rescue experiments, for example replacing JUN with ATF3 or JUNB, to test whether memory depends on a specific heterodimer's stability or DNA-binding properties.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage tracing with live AP-1 reporters (tests population and heritability assumptions)
description: Use a live FOS or ATF3 transcriptional reporter together with a lineage barcode or nuclear label, and image cells over several divisions after a pulse. Measure whether memory is heterogeneous across the population, whether sister cells are correlated, and whether memory passes through mitosis. Pair this with HaloTag-JUN imaging on mitotic chromosomes to test mitotic bookmarking directly.

question: ap1
title: Enhancer AP-1 site knock-in to separate chromatin from feedback (tests the storage-medium assumption)
description: Use CRISPR knock-in to mutate the AP-1 motifs in the endogenous autoregulatory enhancer (for example, the FOS or ATF3 enhancer) while leaving the chromatin context intact, then compare acute induction and rechallenge memory. If memory is lost while baseline chromatin accessibility persists, memory depends on AP-1 binding and positive feedback. If memory persists, the chromatin landscape is the store, and AP-1 only reads it out.

question: ap1
title: Dimer-resolved occupancy after a priming pulse
description: Tests the unitary-AP-1 assumption. Use CUT&Tag or CUT&RUN with knock-in tags for FOS, JUN, and ATF3 at several times after stimulus washout to see whether the sites that stay bound are occupied by a distinct dimer composition, which would identify the memory-bearing complex.

question: ap1
title: Savings-based memory assay across rest intervals
description: Tests the undefined-memory assumption by defining memory operationally as 'savings': prime cells with a fixed pulse, rest from hours to days, then re-stimulate and measure re-induction speed and amplitude of AP-1 targets. Plot savings against rest time and compare it with the decay of AP-1 occupancy to see whether memory outlasts binding.

question: ap1
title: Acute degradation of FOS/JUN after priming
description: Tests whether memory requires persistent AP-1 protein. Use dTAG or auxin-degron knock-ins to deplete FOS and JUN at defined times after a priming pulse, then re-stimulate: retained savings implies storage in chromatin or other marks, while loss implies the protein itself is required. Pair with ATAC-seq and H3K27ac to identify what persists.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage-tracked reporter for an AP-1 enhancer
description: Tests the population-average assumption. Build a knock-in destabilized fluorescent reporter at an AP-1-responsive enhancer, pulse cells, sort by reporter state after rest, and track daughter cells by live imaging over several generations to test whether memory is bimodal and inherited across divisions.

question: ap1
title: Locus-specific necessity and sufficiency of AP-1 binding
description: Tests whether AP-1 is causal rather than a readout. Use base editing to mutate only the TRE motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and separately tether a dimerizable or dCas9-fused AP-1 activator to one enhancer without upstream signal; if synthetic activity recreates the savings phenotype and motif mutation abolishes it, AP-1 is causal at that locus.

question: ap1
title: Time-windowed AP-1 degradation (dTAG/AID) to separate trigger from store
description: Acutely degrade c-Fos or JunB with a degron during priming only, during the washout interval, or only at re-stimulation, then measure re-induction kinetics and enhancer accessibility (ATAC-seq, H3K27ac) at each window. If memory survives loss of AP-1 during washout while chromatin marks persist, the store is chromatin rather than AP-1 itself. This tests the assumption that AP-1 must persist to hold memory.

question: ap1
title: Live single-cell reporter tracking through divisions
description: Knock a fluorescent reporter into an AP-1 target locus (e.g., FOSL1 or an enhancer-driven reporter) and track primed and naive cells by time-lapse microscopy across several generations after washout. Quantify whether the faster re-induction state is bimodal and whether it is inherited by daughter cells (sibling and lineage correlations). This tests population averaging and mitotic heritability.

question: ap1
title: Subunit-resolved occupancy and combinatorial knockouts
description: Use CUT&Tag or ChIP for each Fos, Jun, and ATF family member at memory-associated enhancers during priming and after washout, then test single and double knockouts or knockdowns of the dominant heterodimer partners. This shows which dimer composition persists and whether compensation hides the phenotype. This tests the uniform-AP-1 and clean-knockout assumptions.

question: ap1
title: Cell-autonomy test with co-culture, transwell, and conditioned medium
description: Prime one population, then co-culture it with naive, differently labeled cells, separate them with a transwell, or transfer conditioned medium, and then measure whether the naive cells acquire faster re-induction. Repeat the experiment in an in vivo or transplant setting to check generalization. If the naive cells acquire the memory, the memory is not cell-intrinsic. This tests the cell-autonomy and context-generalization assumptions.

question: ap1
title: Priming-history encoding matrix with mutual information
description: Systematically vary priming dose, pulse duration, pulse frequency, and interval, and measure re-stimulation response at multiple decay timepoints. Compute the mutual information between priming history and the response to determine how much information the AP-1 system stores and for how long. This tests the single-stimulus, single-timescale, and fixed-definition assumptions.

question: ap1
title: Degron-based maintenance test after stimulus washout
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron on endogenous c-Fos or JUNB, then stimulate, wash out, and degrade AP-1 at different times after the pulse. Track enhancer accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target transcription to see whether persistence requires continued AP-1 presence, and compare with histone-mark readouts (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) to separate AP-1-dependent maintenance from chromatin-encoded memory.

question: ap1
title: Paralog- and dimer-specific memory dissection
description: Apply paralog-specific degrons or CRISPR knockouts (e.g., FOS vs FOSB, FOSL1 vs FOSL2, JUNB vs c-JUN, ATF3) and run CUT&Tag for each member after a pulse. Determine which dimer combinations occupy memory-associated enhancers after the stimulus is removed and whether losing one member abolishes persistence.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell live reporter and lineage tracing of persistence
description: Build a destabilized fluorescent reporter driven by an AP-1-responsive enhancer and track individual cells through repeated pulses with time-lapse imaging. Quantify bimodality, the fraction of cells that retain a primed state, and whether the state is inherited by daughter cells, to check whether memory is a subpopulation phenomenon hidden in bulk data.

question: ap1
title: Inducible AP-1 sufficiency without the upstream stimulus
description: Use an optogenetic or chemically inducible AP-1 construct (for example, a light-controlled Fos/Jun heterodimer) to drive AP-1 activity in the absence of the native signal, with matched total-activity controls. Test whether defined pulses of AP-1 activity alone generate a primed state that enhances later responses, separating AP-1 memory from memory held in upstream MAPK/ERK signaling.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic persistence and inheritance timing
description: Synchronize cells after a pulse, then track AP-1 occupancy (live-cell imaging of tagged AP-1 or CUT&RUN at defined mitotic stages) and enhancer accessibility through mitosis and into G1 over several cell cycles. Measure whether the primed state is retained through mitotic chromatin disruption and how long it lasts, which distinguishes heritable memory from a state that must be rebuilt after each division.

question: ap1
title: Degron-timed necessity test during the rest window (tests A3)
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUNB with an auxin-inducible degron and degrade the protein only during the quiescent interval after priming, then measure re-stimulation kinetics and AP-1 occupancy by CUT&RUN. If the memory is lost, the protein itself carries it; if it survives, the carrier is chromatin or another factor.

question: ap1
title: Subunit-by-subunit knockout and rescue (tests A2)
description: Knock out individual AP-1 members (FOS, FOSB, FOSL1, FOSL2, JUN, JUNB, JUND, ATF3) in a priming paradigm, then rescue with wild-type or DNA-binding and dimerization-mutant variants. This shows which subunits and dimer combinations are required for the memory-dependent faster re-induction of target genes.

question: ap1
title: Live single-cell reporter tracking across divisions (tests A4 and A5)
description: Express a destabilized fluorescent reporter driven by an AP-1-responsive promoter and track individual cells by time-lapse microscopy through priming, rest and re-stimulation. Compare the fraction of cells that retain the primed state and whether the state is inherited by daughter cells, to determine whether memory is a subpopulation or heritable property.

question: ap1
title: Cross-stimulus priming with orthogonal pathway controls (tests A7 and A8)
description: Prime cells with two stimuli that converge on AP-1 through different upstream routes (for example phorbol ester versus EGF versus a stress stimulus), then cross-challenge each. Include MEK inhibitor and NF-kB or STAT inhibitor arms and profile their target genes, to see whether the memory encodes stimulus identity specifically and is AP-1-dependent rather than a generic activation signature.

question: ap1
title: Sufficiency test via controlled ectopic AP-1 pulse (tests A6)
description: Induce a defined dose and duration of c-Jun or c-Fos with a dox-inducible or optogenetic clustering system, bypassing the upstream signal entirely, and measure whether the same persistent priming signature appears at endogenous targets upon later challenge. If an artificial pulse is sufficient, AP-1 is the rate-limiting memory node; if it is not, the memory needs upstream signaling.

question: ap1
title: Subunit-resolved, time-gated degradation of AP-1 members
description: Tag endogenous c-Fos, FosB, JunB, c-Jun, and ATF3 with dTAG or AID degrons and degrade each one individually, and in combination, only during the quiescent interval after priming, then measure recall. This identifies which dimers are necessary for memory, exposes compensation, and avoids confounds from constitutive loss (Assumptions 1, 7).

question: ap1
title: Hold-period AP-1 degradation to separate trigger from substrate
description: After priming, degrade AP-1 during the rest period, not during re-stimulation, and track chromatin accessibility, H3K27ac, CUT&RUN occupancy, and recall over time. If primed chromatin persists without AP-1 and recall is intact, the memory lies in chromatin; if recall fails, AP-1 itself is the persistent substrate (Assumptions 2, 4).

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 activity across divisions
description: Use a destabilized fluorescent AP-1 activity reporter with live imaging and tracking across divisions, paired with single-cell multiome readouts. Test whether the primed state is bimodal, whether mother and daughter cells share it, and whether it predicts later recall at single-cell resolution (Assumptions 3, 6).

question: ap1
title: Synthetic AP-1 tethering with washout to test sufficiency and specificity
description: Recruit the c-Jun activation domain or full c-Jun to a silent enhancer or promoter with dCas9 or optogenetic CRY2/CIB, then wash out the tether and test for a persistent primed state. Run the same design with NF-kB, C/EBP, or STAT tethers as controls, and complement with motif mutations at endogenous enhancers (Assumption 5).

question: ap1
title: In vivo engram-style tagging with repeated, patterned stimulation
description: Use Fos-TRAP2 or an AP-1-responsive reporter mouse to permanently label cells activated by a defined stimulus, then re-expose the animal weeks later and measure reactivation of the tagged ensemble, transcriptional priming, and chromatin state. Vary dose, duration, and frequency of the initial stimulus to test whether the memory encodes input patterns (Assumptions 8, 9).

question: ap1
title: Paralog-specific acute degradation (tests assumption 1: AP-1 as one unit)
description: Knock in auxin-inducible degron tags to endogenous Fra1, c-Fos, JunB and Jun, then degrade each member separately after priming. Measure which paralog is required for retention of accessibility and re-induction at memory loci, and test whether swapping in another family member rescues the memory.

question: ap1
title: Remove AP-1 during the washout window (tests assumption 2: AP-1 as the carrier)
description: After priming, use a degron to acutely evict AP-1 during the post-stimulus interval, then track chromatin accessibility, H3K27ac/H3K4me1 by CUT&Tag, and re-induction on re-stimulation. Persistence of marks without AP-1 would indicate chromatin-encoded memory, while loss would indicate that AP-1 maintains the state.

question: ap1
title: Kinetic washout and re-stimulation series (tests assumption 3: persistence vs. altered responsiveness)
description: Vary pulse number and duration, then re-stimulate at a graded series of intervals. Score memory as a stimulus-specific change in re-induction speed or amplitude that decays with a measurable time constant, with a non-AP-1 stimulus and an unrelated TF as controls.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage-traced AP-1 reporter (tests assumption 4: uniform bulk-average state)
description: Knock in a destabilised fluorescent reporter at an AP-1-responsive locus and pair time-lapse imaging with single-cell multiome. Sort daughter pairs and sibling versus unrelated cells to test whether the memory state is bimodal and heritable across divisions.

question: ap1
title: In vivo repeated exposure with ex vivo recall (tests assumption 5: cell-autonomy and in vitro generalisability)
description: In a tissue model with repeated natural stimulation (e.g., repeated injury or mechanical load), lineage-trace AP-1-responsive cells, then isolate them for ex vivo re-stimulation and CUT&Tag. Compare with naive cells and with conditional AP-1 deletion in a mosaic subset to test whether memory is cell-intrinsic and niche-independent.

question: ap1
title: Paralog degron matrix to resolve which AP-1 members carry memory (tests assumption 1)
description: Knock in dTAG or AID degrons to JUN, JUNB, JUND, FOS, FOSL1/2, and ATF3, then degrade individual and combinatorial subsets at defined windows after a priming stimulus and washout. Measure ATAC, H3K27ac, and re-induction of primed genes to find which paralog set is required for memory, rather than assuming AP-1 acts as a single unit.

question: ap1
title: Occupancy-versus-chromatin decoupling by single-molecule tracking and CUT&RUN during washout (tests assumption 3)
description: Use HaloTag-JUN or FOS single-molecule tracking to measure residence time, and CUT&RUN to track occupancy at primed enhancers over the washout time course. If accessibility or H3K27ac at these loci persists after AP-1 unbinds, the carrier is a chromatin state, not AP-1 occupancy, and this can be tested further with pioneer- or acetylation-deficient AP-1 mutants.

question: ap1
title: Two-pulse savings assay with single-cell quantification (tests assumption 4)
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, vary the rest interval, then re-stimulate and quantify lag, amplitude, and magnitude of re-induction for AP-1 targets by smFISH or single-cell RT-qPCR. Repeat with AP-1 degraded during the rest period; memory is defined as a savings effect that depends on AP-1 presence, not as a persistent marker.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-resolved memory tracing across divisions (tests assumptions 5 and 6)
description: Combine CRISPR lineage barcodes with a recorder of prior AP-1 activity, such as a Fos-promoter-driven recombinase or stable reporter, and follow clonal lineages through several divisions. Single-cell multiome readouts will show whether the primed state is inherited within clones, and whether it is uniform or confined to a subpopulation.

question: ap1
title: In vivo engram-style tagging and necessity test in tissue (tests assumption 7)
description: Use Fos-CreERT2 or TRAP labeling to mark cells with AP-1 activity during a repeated physiological stimulus in mouse tissue, such as neurons or trained macrophages. Sort tagged cells at several post-stimulus intervals for ATAC or CUT&Tag, then test necessity by inducing a dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS or TAM67) during the consolidation window and checking whether the memory signature and later reactivation response disappear.

question: ap1
title: Persistence of AP-1 chromatin opening after stimulus withdrawal
description: Mine public stimulus-washout ATAC-seq or H3K27ac time courses (e.g., ENCODE, GEO, ImmGen) to ask whether AP-1 motif sites stay open after the signal is removed, and whether that persistence exceeds that of matched non-AP-1 enhancers. Compare the decay half-lives of AP-1 and non-AP-1 sites to test whether AP-1 specifically confers memory.

question: ap1
title: Re-stimulation kinetics in public sequential-challenge datasets
description: Use public datasets with primary and secondary challenges (for example, memory versus naive T cells, trained-immunity macrophages, or repeated-stimulation fibroblasts) to test whether AP-1 activity at the first exposure predicts faster or stronger gene induction on re-exposure. Control for baseline chromatin state and for the effector or differentiation state of each cell population.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell test of AP-1 accessibility as a predictor of memory state
description: Analyze public single-cell multiome (scRNA plus scATAC) datasets from infection, tumor, or inflammation models to ask whether the AP-1 motif accessibility score in a cell predicts its membership in a memory-like versus terminally differentiated state. Check whether the association holds after conditioning on lineage markers and on the cell's stimulation history.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis analysis of AP-1 target genes in time-resolved expression data
description: Fit bistable or hysteresis models to public time-course RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data with stimulus up-ramps and down-ramps to test whether AP-1 target genes show different on and off thresholds, which would indicate path-dependent memory. Compare the fit with that for targets of other immediate-early factors such as NF-kB or STAT.

question: ap1
title: Loss-of-function evidence from public AP-1 perturbation screens
description: Mine public CRISPR knockout and Perturb-seq resources (such as DepMap, Perturb-seq atlases, and knockout data for JUN, FOS, BATF, and ATF3) to test whether loss of AP-1 components abolishes the transcriptional carry-over that follows a prior stimulus. Include appropriate controls for proliferation and cell death, and check whether the effect is specific to AP-1 targets.

question: ap1
title: Washout time-course of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin state
description: After a defined AP-1-inducing stimulus (e.g., TPA or serum), wash out and profile c-Fos/JunB/ATF3 occupancy (CUT&Tag) alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac at days 0 to 7. Memory is supported if enhancers stay open and retain AP-1 binding or priming marks after the TF signal has returned to baseline. Estimated cost: about $8k to $12k for a single cell line with 6 timepoints in duplicate.

question: ap1
title: Acute degron-mediated necessity test during the memory window
description: Tag endogenous FOS or JUN with an auxin-inducible degron, prime cells, then degrade the factor only during the quiescent interval before re-stimulation. If AP-1 is the memory store, degradation should abolish faster or amplified re-induction of primed target genes (measured by RT-qPCR/RNA-seq) without affecting the naive response. Estimated cost: about $10k to $15k for knock-in, validation, and RNA-seq.

question: ap1
title: Base-editing of AP-1 motifs at endogenous primed enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editors or prime editors to mutate the TRE/AP-1 motifs in 3 to 5 enhancers that show memory-like priming, then compare primed-state accessibility and re-stimulation kinetics in edited versus control clones. This tests whether the specific motif sites, rather than general AP-1 presence, carry the memory. Estimated cost: about $9k to $14k for guide design, clone isolation, and ATAC/RNA readouts.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell reporter lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Build a destabilized-fluorescent-protein reporter driven by an AP-1-responsive enhancer and track individual cells by time-lapse microscopy through several divisions after a pulse of stimulus. Memory is supported if the re-induction response is heritable in daughter cells and decays on a timescale matching the chromatin persistence measured elsewhere. Estimated cost: about $5k to $9k for the lentiviral reporter, imaging, and analysis.

question: ap1
title: Protein-synthesis block and mitotic bookmarking assay
description: Pulse stimulus, then add cycloheximide or a translation inhibitor to remove newly made AP-1 protein, and use mitotic-cell CUT&Tag or ChIP to test whether AP-1 stays bound on condensed chromatin through mitosis. Retention of AP-1 at memory enhancers without de novo synthesis would show self-sustaining, bookmarking-like memory, while loss would point to protein turnover as the main driver. Estimated cost: about $4k to $7k for the inhibitor experiments, sorted mitotic cells, and sequencing.

question: ap1
title: Washout persistence as a function of pulse duration
description: Expose cells carrying a live AP-1 transcriptional reporter (for example, a destabilized fluorescent protein under AP-1 response elements) to stimulus pulses of varying length, then wash out and track reporter decay for days. Memory is supported if the persistence time scales with pulse duration and outlasts the reporter's protein turnover and the stimulus clearance.

question: ap1
title: Savings test with varied inter-pulse intervals
description: Give two stimulus pulses separated by different rest intervals and compare the second response's latency, amplitude, and duration with the first using endogenous AP-1 subunit tags (e.g., JUNB or FOSL1 knock-in fluorescent fusions). A faster or stronger second response that decays with longer intervals is a direct, quantifiable signature of memory.

question: ap1
title: Heritability of AP-1 state across cell divisions
description: Stimulate cells, remove the stimulus, and track lineages with a nuclear marker while recording the AP-1 reporter in each cell and its daughters. Quantify how well the pre-division state predicts daughter states (lineage autocorrelation), since carrying AP-1 activity through divisions would indicate a heritable memory rather than a signal-dependent state.

question: ap1
title: Degron-based causal test during the memory window
description: Once persistent AP-1 activity is established, use an inducible degradation tag (e.g., auxin or dTAG) on a JUN or FOS subunit to remove the protein while following the reporter in real time. If the persistent state collapses on degradation, AP-1 is necessary to maintain it, while persistence after degradation would argue against it being the memory store.

question: ap1
title: Chromatin residence time of AP-1 after stimulus removal
description: Use HaloTag-labeled JUN or FOS with live-cell FRAP or single-molecule tracking to measure how long AP-1 remains bound to chromatin after stimulus withdrawal and how that residence time changes over days. A residence time that stays elevated after the signal ends would provide a molecular, binding-level readout of memory.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-washout chromatin time course
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., TPA, EGF, or serum) for varying pulse lengths, wash out, and profile endogenous c-Fos/JunB occupancy (CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq) alongside chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and H3K27ac over days. If AP-1 acts as memory, enhancer accessibility and activity should persist after AP-1 occupancy decays, and a second stimulus should trigger a faster or stronger response at those same sites.

question: ap1
title: Time-gated small-molecule inhibition
description: Apply AP-1 pathway inhibitors (e.g., the c-Jun/AP-1 DNA-binding inhibitor T-5224) or upstream JNK/ERK inhibitors only before, during, or after a priming stimulus, then measure chromatin state and re-stimulated transcription. Inhibition during the priming window versus after it separates whether AP-1 is needed to establish a memory versus maintain it, with the caveat that small-molecule specificity must be validated with dose-response and orthogonal readouts.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell history-dependence with multiplexed imaging
description: Prime cells with varying stimulus histories, then use cyclic immunofluorescence or multiplexed smFISH on endogenous FOS, JUN, and downstream targets to measure per-cell AP-1 levels and response to a challenge stimulus. Testing whether a cell's prior AP-1 history predicts its challenge response, beyond population averages, is a direct test of cell-intrinsic memory.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic persistence of AP-1-bound sites
description: Sort or synchronize cells in mitosis after priming and compare AP-1 occupancy and accessibility on mitotic chromatin to interphase, asking whether AP-1 bookmarks the same enhancers. Then track whether the post-mitotic daughters retain the primed state across several divisions after stimulus removal, which tests whether AP-1 memory is heritable through cell division.

question: ap1
title: Natural variation and trained-immunity cohort
description: Use primary monocytes or iPSC-derived macrophages from genetically diverse donors, stimulated with a trained-immunity inducer (e.g., β-glucan) and then re-challenged after a rest period. Correlate AP-1 binding strength and allele-specific AP-1 occupancy at heterozygous sites with the magnitude and duration of the trained response, using natural genetic variation rather than engineered perturbation to test whether AP-1 binding causally predicts memory.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-washout with reactivation kinetics in Drosophila S2 cells
description: Induce a defined AP-1 (Jun/Fos or Kayak/Jra) pulse with an inducible system, wash it out, and track target-gene expression, AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN), and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 at enhancers over days. Re-stimulate after washout and test whether faster or stronger re-induction persists, then repeat with TRE-mutated enhancers to show the memory depends on AP-1 binding rather than on the stimulus alone.

question: ap1
title: Tethered-AP-1 sufficiency test using dCas9 or dCas13 in Drosophila cells
description: Use a dCas9-based or synthetic zinc-finger tether to recruit Jun or Fos to a silent reporter locus for a short window, then release it and measure whether the locus stays primed (chromatin opening, Pol II poising, reporter expression on re-challenge). Compare against tethers of an unrelated transcription factor to show that AP-1 specifically writes a persistent state, not just transient activation.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage tracking of repeated stress pulses in yeast
description: In S. cerevisiae carrying an AP-1-like bZIP (Yap1) or a heterologous Jun/Fos, use microfluidic time-lapse imaging of a fluorescent reporter across repeated stress pulses with varying intervals. Quantify whether cells that experienced a prior pulse respond faster on the next exposure, whether memory decays with interval, and whether it is lost with an auxin- or anchor-away-mediated depletion of the factor or with binding-site mutations.

question: ap1
title: Learning-dependent AP-1 requirement in C. elegans behavior
description: Train worms in a pathogen-avoidance or aversive olfactory paradigm while knocking down jun-1 or fos-1 with a temporally controlled degron or heat-shock promoter, separating the training window from the retention interval and recall test. Pair this with calcium imaging of the relevant interneurons and neuron-specific rescue to determine whether AP-1 is needed for acquisition, consolidation, or retention.

question: ap1
title: Injury-priming test of AP-1 enhancers during zebrafish regeneration
description: Perform a first fin amputation, allow recovery, then re-amputate and compare regeneration speed and fos/jun enhancer reporter activity with naive fish. Use scATAC-seq or single-cell RNA-seq at the second injury to identify primed cell states, and CRISPR knockout of jun or fos paralogs to test whether the faster second response, and the enhancer's persistent accessibility between injuries, depends on AP-1.

question: ap1
title: Degron-based AP-1 washout and rechallenge
description: Use a dTAG or auxin-inducible degron on endogenous c-Jun or c-Fos in primary cells or a cell line. Give a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, EGF, or LPS), wash out, and let cells rest for 1-2 weeks, with or without AP-1 depletion during the rest period. Then restimulate and measure the speed and magnitude of target-gene induction by RT-qPCR or RNA-seq. If memory requires AP-1 persistence, the faster response should be lost when AP-1 is degraded during rest.

question: ap1
title: Time-resolved CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq across a stimulus-rest cycle
description: Profile AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for c-Fos, JunB, ATF3), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and H3K27ac at multiple timepoints through stimulation, washout, and the quiescent interval. Test whether enhancers that stay accessible or acetylated after AP-1 leaves the chromatin predict the rechallenge response. Pair this with the degron approach to separate AP-1-dependent retention from chromatin-intrinsic retention.

question: ap1
title: Live single-cell reporter of AP-1 activity across repeated pulses
description: Build a destabilized fluorescent reporter driven by an AP-1-responsive promoter, or knock a reporter into an endogenous AP-1 target such as FOS or ATF3, and track individual cells by live imaging or microfluidics. Apply pulses at varied intervals and quantify, per cell, whether the second response is faster or larger than the first. Correlate memory with nuclear c-Jun or c-Fos levels and their persistence to test whether memory is a graded, cell-autonomous property.

question: ap1
title: Enhancer motif mutagenesis to test necessity of AP-1 binding for memory
description: Using CRISPR knock-in or base editing, mutate the AP-1 (TGAnTCA) sites in one or several memory-associated enhancers identified from the CUT&RUN data, or use dCas9-KRAB to block binding at those sites. Compare the primed response to rechallenge in wild-type and mutant clones, and include a non-AP-1 control enhancer. This is a direct test of whether the specific AP-1 sites are necessary for the memory, not just correlated with it.

question: ap1
title: Fos-TRAP lineage tagging of AP-1-experienced cells in vivo
description: Use existing Fos-CreERT2 reporter mice to permanently label cells that were AP-1-active during a defined stimulus, such as a skin irritant, tissue injury, or an inflammatory challenge. After a rest period, rechallenge the animals and measure whether tagged cells show enhanced reactivation of AP-1 targets compared with untagged neighbors, by flow cytometry or spatial transcriptomics. This tests whether AP-1 history marks cells for altered future responses in a physiological setting.

question: ap1
title: Chromatin persistence at AP-1 enhancers after signal washout
description: Give a transient stimulus, then harvest separate animal or cell cohorts at different washout intervals, each sampled once by ATAC-seq or CUT&Tag for H3K27ac and AP-1 (Fos/Jun) occupancy. If AP-1-bound enhancers stay open or acetylated after c-Fos/JunB protein returns to baseline, that supports a chromatin-based memory rather than a transient signaling response.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell multiome linking prior exposure to a later response
description: Split a population into groups with different prior AP-1-activating histories, then challenge each group with a standard stimulus and collect one multiome snapshot per sample at the response peak. Test whether residual AP-1 motif accessibility before the challenge predicts the magnitude and speed of the secondary target-gene induction, and whether that predictive signal is absent in cells lacking the pre-exposure.

question: ap1
title: Necessity test with AP-1 loss-of-function in a persistence readout
description: Compare the persistent chromatin and transcriptional state at a single late timepoint in wild-type cells versus cells with Fos or Jun knockdown, dominant-negative A-FOS/TAM67 expression, or conditional deletion, each sampled once after the same stimulus history. If the persistent enhancer marks or memory-associated gene expression disappear without AP-1, AP-1 is required rather than merely correlated with memory.

question: ap1
title: Decoupling AP-1 protein decay from chromatin memory
description: Use mass cytometry or phospho/intracellular flow to measure c-Fos, JunB and other AP-1 protein levels in single cells across a series of washout durations, with each cell measured once. A mismatch in which AP-1 protein returns to baseline while chromatin marks or target-gene poised states remain elevated would separate a durable mnemonic state from ongoing AP-1 signaling.

question: ap1
title: Ex vivo re-stimulation of explants harvested after in vivo experience
description: Expose animals to a single in vivo stimulus, then at a fixed later time harvest tissue explants and stimulate each one ex vivo with the same challenge, fixing each explant once for AP-1 target-gene and AP-1 motif-enhancer readouts. Explants from experienced animals that show faster or stronger AP-1 target induction than naive controls would indicate a latent, cell-intrinsic memory that survives tissue removal from the original context.

question: ap1
title: Longitudinal chromatin profiling of patient biopsies across a stimulus cycle
description: Collect paired biopsies or blood samples from the same patients at baseline, peak activation, and after resolution, then run ATAC-seq and FOS/JUN CUT&RUN. Memory predicts that AP-1 motif accessibility and JUN/FOS occupancy stay elevated at loci induced during the flare even after clinical and transcriptional markers return to baseline, and that this persistence is specific to AP-1 motifs compared with matched control motifs such as CEBP or RUNX.

question: ap1
title: Ex vivo stimulus washout and re-challenge in patient-derived primary cells
description: Stimulate patient-derived monocytes, T cells, or fibroblasts with a defined AP-1-inducing signal, wash out for several days, then re-challenge and measure the speed and magnitude of AP-1 target gene induction (for example by RNA-seq time courses and nascent transcription). Memory is supported if re-challenged cells respond faster or more strongly than naive cells from the same donor, and the effect is abolished by a pharmacological AP-1 inhibitor or by a degron-based JUN knockdown.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-chase single-cell multiome in patient-derived organoids
description: Treat patient-derived organoids with a transient pulse of a stimulus or drug, then profile them with single-cell multiome (scRNA plus scATAC) at multiple times after washout. Track whether AP-1-linked open chromatin persists in specific cell states and whether those states show a faster transcriptional response to a second pulse, using per-cell barcoding to link memory state to later response.

question: ap1
title: Persister-cell tracking across therapy and drug holiday in patient tumor samples
description: Obtain matched tumor samples before treatment, during treatment, and at relapse after a drug holiday, and use scATAC-seq and lineage barcodes to follow the same clones over time. Test whether AP-1-accessible persister states that survive therapy are re-enriched at relapse and whether they show a faster re-induction of AP-1 targets than treatment-naive clones, which would support AP-1 as a memory of prior drug exposure.

question: ap1
title: Locus-specific necessity test with dCas9 epigenome editing in patient-derived cells
description: In patient-derived cells, use dCas9 fused to a p300 activator or KRAB repressor to open or close AP-1 sites at selected memory loci, then remove the effector and track chromatin state and transcription over time. If AP-1 is the memory mechanism, the edited state should persist after effector removal only when the AP-1 motif is intact, which can be tested by pairing each site with a motif-mutant control.

question: ap1
title: Single-molecule residence-time tracking of JUN/FOS after a pulse
description: Use HaloTag-labeled JUN or FOS in live cells with single-molecule tracking to measure chromatin dwell-time distributions before, during, and for days after a stimulus. A persistent long-dwell bound fraction that outlasts the pulse, without any change in total protein level, would suggest memory is stored as altered factor kinetics rather than as a new steady-state binding pattern.

question: ap1
title: Phosphosite knock-in swaps to test whether post-translational state carries memory
description: Knock in phosphomimetic and phospho-dead alleles at key JUN and FOS regulatory sites (for example JUN Ser63/Ser73), then use phospho-specific mass spectrometry and washout time courses to track how long each modification persists. If the memory-related transcriptional response tracks the phospho-state rather than AP-1 protein abundance or occupancy, the modification itself is the stored variable.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-chase separation of carryover from chromatin memory
description: Combine SLAM-seq or 4sU pulse-chase labeling with transcription inhibition (such as flavopiridol or triptolide) applied at defined washout times, and then re-stimulate. Persistence that survives transcriptional shutdown would point to carryover of mRNA or protein, while loss of memory under shutdown would indicate that new transcription is needed to maintain the state.

question: ap1
title: Kinase-route coding test with orthogonal upstream stimuli
description: Prime cells with equivalent AP-1 induction achieved through different upstream routes (ERK, JNK, or p38, using pathway-selective stimuli or inhibitors) and then cross-challenge with each route. If reinduction is pathway-specific despite similar AP-1 levels, the memory encodes the signaling route, not the transcription factor level, which would make AP-1 a readout rather than the storage element.

question: ap1
title: Coactivator-tethering rescue in a JUN-null background
description: Replace endogenous JUN with variants that have matched DNA-binding but differ in their ability to recruit BRD4 or p300/CBP, and measure how long induced enhancer acetylation and target expression persist after washout. If memory duration tracks coactivator recruitment rather than AP-1 occupancy, the persistence mechanism depends on the coactivator feedback loop rather than on the AP-1 complex itself.

question: ap1
title: Parental histone inheritance through replication
description: Pulse-label pre-existing H3.3 with SNAP or Halo tags before and after a stimulus, then follow the old-versus-new histone ratio at AP-1 enhancers through one or two cell divisions. If AP-1 memory rides on nucleosome inheritance, the old, stimulus-era histones should stay enriched at these enhancers in daughter cells, and blocking histone recycling (for example, with MCM2 or FACT perturbation) should erase the primed state.

question: ap1
title: Paused Pol II as the stored state
description: Use PRO-seq or GRO-seq during washout to measure promoter-proximal Pol II pausing at AP-1 target genes, and ask whether paused polymerase persists after AP-1 has left the enhancer. A memory mechanism predicts faster pause release on restimulation, and this effect should be blocked by a transient CDK9 or P-TEFb inhibitor applied only during the rest period.

question: ap1
title: Partner-switching readout of the AP-1 dimer
description: Use TurboID or APEX proximity labeling on FOS and JUN at several washout times to test whether repressive partners such as ATF3, JDP2, or JUNB take over the dimer slot after the stimulus. Then knock out the substitute partner and test whether recall is altered, which would show that memory depends on the composition of the dimer rather than on its presence.

question: ap1
title: Nuclear-periphery relocalization of primed loci
description: Label an AP-1 target locus with an ANCHOR or ParB array and track its distance to the nuclear lamina and nuclear pore complexes by live imaging across stimulus and rest periods. Persistent pore association after the stimulus, which disappears in cells with nuclear pore anchoring mutants, would indicate that spatial repositioning stores the memory.

question: ap1
title: Cross-stimulus priming matrix to define memory specificity
description: Prime cells with a set of stimuli that act through AP-1 alone, through NF-kB, or through cAMP-CREB, then measure the response to every restimulation pairing with an AP-1-dependent reporter. A genuine AP-1 memory should show a specific pattern of cross-priming that tracks the AP-1 binding sites of each stimulus and disappears when those sites are mutated, which is a more discriminating test than asking whether any memory exists.

question: ap1
title: Heterokaryon nuclear swap to locate the memory
description: Fuse primed cells with naive cells, or use chemically induced nuclear transfer, to create shared cytoplasm containing one primed and one naive nucleus. If the naive nucleus becomes re-inducible while the primed nucleus keeps its advantage, memory is nuclear-intrinsic; if the state spreads through the shared cytoplasm, it is a diffusible signaling or protein-pool property.

question: ap1
title: Parental histone inheritance at AP-1 enhancers
description: Label pre-existing H3 or H3.3 with a SNAP/Halo tag, pulse with AP-1 stimulus, then chase through one or two divisions and use quantitative CUT&Tag to measure whether old versus newly synthesized histones are retained at primed enhancers. Preferential retention of old histones at AP-1-bound sites would suggest that memory is carried by histone recycling rather than by the TF itself.

question: ap1
title: Transcription-dependent versus binding-dependent memory
description: Use CRISPRi with dCas9-KRAB or a promoter-directed transcriptional-interference strategy to silence eRNA or nascent transcription at primed enhancers while leaving c-Jun or Fos occupancy intact, and separately block the transcription of the memory gene itself. Dissociating occupancy from ongoing transcription would show whether the memory requires active transcription in the quiescent phase or only a stable bound configuration.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-pattern decoding with microfluidic stimulation
description: Expose cells to AP-1-inducing stimuli in microfluidic devices with systematically varied pulse number, duty cycle, and inter-pulse interval, then measure re-induction after a fixed rest. Fitting the resulting response surface would reveal whether memory encodes integrated dose, pulse count, or timing, and would give a quantitative rule that a mechanistic model must reproduce.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-chase proteomics of AP-1 dimer stoichiometry
description: Use SILAC or a tagged pulse-chase to measure half-lives and heterodimer composition of Fos, Jun, JunB, and ATF3 after stimulation, quantified by immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry at several time points. A stimulus-induced shift toward long-lived, stable dimer partners during quiescence would identify a protein-level memory that can be tested for necessity directly.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic bookmarking and sister-cell inheritance of a primed state
description: Use HaloTag-tagged c-Jun or c-Fos with single-molecule tracking through mitosis to test whether AP-1 stays on mitotic chromosomes after a pulse, then compare re-induction kinetics between sister cells that inherit the same pulse history. If the primed state is inherited by both sisters without ongoing AP-1, that supports bookmarking-based memory rather than a per-cell state that resets at division.

question: ap1
title: Nucleosome turnover pulse-chase at AP-1-bound enhancers
description: Express SNAP-tagged H3.3 (or H2A.Z) and measure nucleosome exchange rates at AP-1-bound versus unbound enhancers during and after a transient stimulus using pulse-chase labeling and ChIP-seq. A memory mechanism would predict that enhancers retaining a primed state show slower nucleosome exchange that persists after AP-1 leaves, which is distinct from simply measuring whether the chromatin mark is present.

question: ap1
title: Protein-lifetime readout of AP-1 memory using fluorescent timers
description: Knock in tandem fluorescent timers (or FAST-tagged versions) to JunB, ATF3, and c-Jun to measure the age and half-life of the chromatin-bound AP-1 pool after a stimulus, and pair this with cycloheximide chase and phospho-proteomics. description: Combine a Fos-driven recombinase or TRAP reporter with a heritable lineage barcode and single-cell multiome (scRNA + scATAC) to tag cells that activated AP-1 during a stimulus. Follow these cells after washout and during re-stimulation to ask whether the tagged subset is a stable, heterogeneous population that responds faster, and whether memory is carried by a minority of cells rather than uniformly across the population.

question: ap1
title: Dilution-independent persistence test across cell divisions and quiescence
description: Label a stimulus-experienced population with a live AP-1 reporter and a division-tracking dye, then separate cells into quiescent and proliferating fractions over a long rest period. Measure whether AP-1-dependent accessibility and priming decay with division, dilution, or time alone, and compare the decay curve with that of stable marks such as DNA methylation or H3K4me1. This separates a true epigenetic memory from a transient signalling state that merely persists while the cell stays alive.

question: ap1
title: Chromatin conformation persistence after AP-1 activity ends
description: Perform Micro-C or Hi-C at AP-1-responsive loci at several timepoints after a stimulus is removed, and pair this with live-cell imaging of locus distance in reporter lines. Test whether enhancer-promoter loops formed by AP-1 remain after AP-1 is no longer bound, and whether these loops are required for faster re-induction. Persistent looping that outlasts AP-1 occupancy would indicate a structural memory layer, and disrupting the loops with CTCF or cohesin depletion would test whether that structure is necessary.

question: ap1
title: Chromatin persistence after stimulus washout (the anchor test)
description: Pulse cells with a transient AP-1 stimulus (e.g., TPA or EGF), then track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for Fos/Jun), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and H3K27ac at each time point after withdrawal. Memory requires the accessibility or enhancer marks to outlast AP-1 binding, just as the spider's thread needs an anchor to hold after it is flung out.

question: ap1
title: Degron-mediated AP-1 removal during the quiescent interval
description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, then use an auxin-inducible or dTAG degron to deplete Fos or Jun during the rest period before a second stimulus. If the faster or stronger re-induction of target genes disappears only when AP-1 is removed in the gap, AP-1 is necessary to carry the memory, not just to read it out.

question: ap1
title: Savings assay with enhancer motif mutants
description: Use CRISPR base editing or prime editing to disrupt individual TRE/AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, then compare primary and secondary responses of nearby genes in wild-type and mutant clones. A memory mechanism predicts that losing a specific motif selectively abolishes the faster secondary response while leaving the first response intact, like a gossamer thread that no longer catches.

question: ap1
title: Heritability of AP-1 state through mitosis
description: Use a knock-in Fos or Jun live reporter with lineage tracking to sort cells by prior AP-1 history and follow them through several divisions, then test whether daughter cells retain the primed response. Live imaging of chromatin binding during mitosis (mitotic bookmarking) will show whether AP-1 stays bound across division, which would make the memory cell-heritable.

question: ap1
title: Single-molecule residence time versus memory duration
description: Measure the chromatin residence time of AP-1 subunits by single-molecule tracking or FRAP in live cells, and pair it with pulse-chase protein half-life measurements (SNAP/HaloTag). Test whether a longer-lived or more stably bound AP-1 population predicts how long the memory lasts across perturbations such as cycloheximide or stabilizing mutants, like the filament that keeps unreeling until it finds a place to hold.

question: ap1
title: Washout time-course of AP-1 occupancy versus chromatin memory
description: After a defined stimulus pulse, remove the stimulus and sample at multiple timepoints with AP-1 (JUN/FOS) CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq. A memory mechanism predicts that accessibility and H3K27ac at AP-1-bound enhancers outlast AP-1 occupancy, while a simple transcriptional readout predicts both decay together; the gap in decay kinetics is the test, much like the 'hour' the early gold leaf lasts before it subsides.

question: ap1
title: Re-stimulation priming assay with a time-gated AP-1 knockdown
description: Give cells a priming stimulus, wait a rest interval, then re-stimulate and measure the speed and magnitude of target gene induction. Use an auxin-inducible degron on JUN or FOS to deplete AP-1 either during the rest interval or only during re-stimulation; if memory relies on AP-1, depleting it during rest should abolish faster re-induction, while depleting it only during re-stimulation should not.

question: ap1
title: Sequential ChIP (re-ChIP) to test whether marks persist after AP-1 leaves
description: Perform sequential ChIP-seq for AP-1 followed by H3K4me1, H3K27ac or H3K4me3 at memory-associated enhancers, comparing primed cells after a rest period against naive cells. If the marks remain at sites where AP-1 is no longer bound, the memory is likely carried by the chromatin state rather than by continued AP-1 occupancy.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell heritability test with an AP-1-responsive lineage barcode
description: Pair an AP-1-responsive reporter (for example an Fos-promoter-driven recombinase or tTA system) with a heritable lineage barcode, then pulse the stimulus and track whether reporter-positive or memory-positive states persist through several cell divisions. Heritable retention across generations without continued stimulation supports a self-maintaining memory, while rapid dilution through divisions supports a transient response.

question: ap1
title: Perturbation of AP-1 partner and co-factor balance during the rest interval
description: Use dominant-negative or ectopic c-Jun/ATF3/JDP2 variants to alter the AP-1 dimer composition during the quiescent window and measure both chromatin accessibility at memory loci and re-induction kinetics. Because different dimers are known to differ in stability and chromatin-opening capacity, a memory mechanism predicts that specific composition shifts change persistence of primed states, while a non-memory, purely reactive role predicts no effect on the rest-period-to-reactivation difference.

question: ap1
title: Chromatin persistence after AP-1 washout
description: Pulse cells with a stimulus, then wash it out and track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for c-Jun/c-Fos) alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac over days.
