question: ap1
title: Acute AP-1 depletion during the inter-stimulus interval
description: Prime cells with one stimulus, then use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on Fos or Jun to remove AP-1 during the rest period before a second stimulus. Memory is defined as a faster or stronger re-induction; if the primed advantage disappears only when AP-1 is degraded during the gap, AP-1 is required to store the memory rather than just to read it out.

question: ap1
title: Mutating AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing to mutate AP-1 motifs on individual primed enhancers, mirroring each mutation on a matched control enhancer to keep the design symmetric. Then measure whether the enhancer's persistence of accessibility, H3K27ac and re-induction kinetics are lost, which tests whether motif occupancy at specific loci is necessary for the memory.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-resolved tracking of primed states through division
description: Combine an AP-1-responsive fluorescent reporter with lineage barcoding and time-lapse imaging to follow single cells after priming. Ask whether the primed state is inherited by daughter cells and whether it fades in the absence of reactivation, which distinguishes a self-sustaining epigenetic memory from a transient signaling state that is simply reset.

question: ap1
title: Protein turnover and bistability modeling
description: Measure the half-lives of Fos, Jun and Fra1 with SNAP/HaloTag pulse-chase and FRAP, then build a kinetic model with and without an AP-1-dependent feedback loop. Test whether the model with a feedback loop predicts a long-lived, bistable primed state that persists for longer than protein turnover alone allows, and whether that prediction holds in the unstimulated dark state.

question: ap1
title: Persistence After Signal Withdrawal (the lake that keeps lapping)
description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus (e.g., TPA, EGF, or LPS), wash it out, and track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for c-Jun/c-Fos), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and nascent transcription (PRO-seq) at target enhancers over days. Memory requires that the altered state outlasts the stimulus, so loci that stay open or bound after the signal is gone are the strongest candidates.

question: ap1
title: Inducible Degron Erasure Test
description: Tag endogenous JUN or FOS with an auxin-inducible degron (e.g., AID2), prime cells, then degrade the factor during the quiescent gap before re-challenge. If AP-1 is the memory store, degradation should erase the primed chromatin state and faster reinduction; if the primed state survives, AP-1 is only a readout of an independent store.

question: ap1
title: Re-stimulation Kinetics at Primed Versus Naive Loci
description: Compare first and second responses to the same stimulus, measuring time-to-peak, fold induction, and the number of activated AP-1 target genes, alongside locus-specific CRISPR deletion or mutation of individual AP-1 motifs. A memory mechanism predicts faster, stronger reinduction that depends on the specific motifs at primed enhancers, not on global AP-1 levels.

question: ap1
title: Single-Cell AP-1 Reporter with Lineage Tracing
description: Build a fast-degrading AP-1 reporter (destabilized fluorescent protein under AP-1 response elements) and track single cells through several divisions after pulses of different duration and frequency. Heritable, history-dependent reporter states that persist across mitosis, and correlate between sister cells, would indicate a stable cellular memory rather than a transient response.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic Inheritance of AP-1-Marked Chromatin
description: Prime cells, arrest them in mitosis, and use mitotic ChIP or ATAC on sorted mitotic cells to test whether AP-1 and its primed accessibility persist on chromosomes through division. Repeat in vivo with a tissue-specific Fos or Jun conditional knockout, priming with a repeated inflammatory or injury stimulus and challenging weeks later, to check whether the memory requires AP-1 at the organismal level.

question: ap1
title: Degron-based AP-1 removal after priming
description: Give a transient stimulus that primes a cell, then use an acute degron system (dTAG or AID) to deplete c-Fos or c-Jun at set times afterward. Measure whether the primed response (faster or stronger reinduction of target genes on a second stimulus) survives AP-1 protein loss. Persistence without AP-1 points to a chromatin-based memory, while loss of the primed state shows AP-1 is required to maintain memory.

question: ap1
title: Time-resolved chromatin persistence at AP-1 sites
description: After one brief stimulus, profile AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for Fos/Jun), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and histone marks such as H3K27ac at multiple time points until AP-1 returns to baseline. Sites that stay open or marked after AP-1 is gone, and that predict faster transcription on re-exposure, are the strongest candidate memory marks. Adding an AP-1 perturbation at this stage separates the marks from the transient binding that caused them.

question: ap1
title: Pattern-dependent optogenetic AP-1 pulsing
description: Use a light-inducible AP-1 construct (e.g., a LOV-domain-controlled Fos/Jun) to deliver pulses that vary in number, frequency, and spacing. Test which temporal patterns produce a lasting primed state and whether the memory depends on pulse history rather than total AP-1 dose. This tests whether AP-1 encodes information in its dynamics, the way Wordsworth's flash of daffodils is remembered by its repeated return rather than by a single glimpse.

question: ap1
title: Activity-tagged ensemble reactivation test
description: Label cells that were AP-1-active during a learning-like stimulus using an activity-dependent reporter (for example, a TRAP-style Fos-CreER system), then re-expose the animal or culture to a partial cue and check whether the tagged cells reactivate preferentially. Compare with animals or cultures carrying a Fos loss-of-function or dominant-negative allele. Selective reactivation of tagged cells that depends on AP-1 function would show that AP-1 marks engram-like memory cells.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell AP-1 history predicts future response
description: Use a live knock-in fluorescent reporter of AP-1 activity to track individual cells through repeated stimuli, recording each cell's prior AP-1 pulse history. Test whether that history predicts the magnitude and speed of the cell's response to a later stimulus, and whether AP-1 inhibitors such as T-5224 erase this predictive relationship. A history-dependent response that disappears with AP-1 inhibition directly links AP-1 activity to cellular memory.

question: ap1
title: Indelibility test with acute AP-1 depletion ("indelibly")
description: Use an inducible degron or auxin-degradable tag on endogenous FOS or JUN to remove AP-1 during a washout window after a priming stimulus, then re-stimulate and compare the second-response gene induction to unperturbed cells. If AP-1 is the memory store, depletion during the interval should erase the faster or stronger re-induction (savings) at its target genes.

question: ap1
title: Time-resolved persistence of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin marks
description: Run CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for FOS/JUN, alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac, at multiple time points during stimulus, washout, and days-long rest. A memory mechanism predicts AP-1 binding or accessibility that outlasts the transcriptional response at a subset of enhancers, and that this persistence tracks the length of the original stimulus.

question: ap1
title: Motif-specific enhancer knock-in ("insulator" logic)
description: Use CRISPR to mutate only the AP-1 motifs in a defined enhancer, or to swap in a non-AP-1 binding site, while keeping the surrounding sequence and nearby transcription factor sites intact. Then measure whether the priming and re-induction behavior is lost, which would show the memory depends on AP-1 binding itself rather than on the locus or on general enhancer activity.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-stable reporter to test cell-state memory across divisions ("sootless" tracing)
description: Combine an activity-dependent Fos reporter or FosTRAP-style recorder with single-cell lineage barcoding, and follow the marked cells through several cell divisions and days after stimulus. If AP-1 maintains a memory, the reporter-positive lineages should keep a primed transcriptional state and faster response even when the AP-1 protein itself has fallen back to baseline.

question: ap1
title: Dissociating protein persistence from mitotic or chromatin bookmarking ("riskless" controls)
description: Pair cycloheximide or other protein-synthesis blockers, and an optogenetic or light-inducible AP-1 nuclear export switch, with the re-stimulation assay to see whether the memory needs ongoing AP-1 protein or only the chromatin state it left behind. Mitotic chromatin retention assays, such as live imaging of AP-1 on mitotic chromosomes, would test whether AP-1 bookmarks its sites through division.

question: ap1
title: Washout and re-stimulation (priming) test
description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus (e.g., TPA or EGF), wash out, and wait through a quiescent interval. Then re-stimulate and compare naive and primed cells by time-resolved RNA-seq and ATAC-seq. Memory is supported if primed cells show faster or stronger induction of AP-1 target genes, and that advantage disappears when the interval is extended or the washout is reversed. The 'undo' step is the control: a true memory should persist after the stimulus is removed.

question: ap1
title: Acute degradation of c-Jun or c-Fos during the quiescent interval
description: Tag endogenous c-Jun or c-Fos with a degron (e.g., dTAG or AID) and degrade it after priming but before re-stimulation. If the primed response survives loss of the AP-1 protein, the memory is stored in chromatin or other marks rather than in the transcription factor itself. If the advantage is lost, AP-1 must be continuously present to maintain the memory.

question: ap1
title: Heritable lineage recording of AP-1 activity history
description: Drive a stable reporter (Cre-loxP switch, or a CRISPR-based cumulative recorder) from AP-1-responsive enhancers so that each past AP-1 activation leaves a permanent, heritable mark. This works like madder staining bone, recording past exposure in the tissue itself. Sorting or imaging cells by mark, then tracking their clonal descendants, tests whether prior AP-1 activity is inherited through divisions and predicts later responses.

question: ap1
title: Motif-level mutagenesis of memory-associated enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or prime editing to mutate the AP-1 motifs in candidate enhancers one at a time, leaving other elements and baseline transcription intact. Then test whether each mutation removes the priming-dependent gain in re-induction without affecting the first response. This separates the role of AP-1 binding in memory from its role in the initial activation, and it works like a primer's cue that is needed only for later recall.

question: ap1
title: Chromatin bookmark persistence with CUT&RUN and epigenetic inhibition
description: Map AP-1 (Fos/Jun family) occupancy and H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and Pol II pausing by CUT&RUN and ChIP-seq at multiple time points after priming, including the quiescent phase. Then inhibit p300/CBP or BRD4 during the interval to test whether retained enhancer marks at those sites are required for faster re-induction. If the memory depends on these marks, blocking their maintenance should erase the primed response while leaving the first response intact.

question: ap1
title: Stimulus washout and chromatin persistence time course
description: Stimulate cells with a defined AP-1 inducer (e.g., TPA or EGF), then withdraw it and profile AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for c-Jun/c-Fos) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) at multiple time points over days. Memory predicts that AP-1 sites stay open or bound after the signal is gone, and this persistence should be compared with sites that return to baseline. The material's 'terminator' suggests framing the washout as the stop signal that separates true memory from ongoing signaling.

question: ap1
title: Re-stimulation test for faster or stronger secondary response
description: Compare naive cells with cells that had a prior stimulus and washout, then re-stimulate both and measure AP-1 target gene induction (RNA-seq or smFISH) and the speed and amplitude of the response. A memory mechanism should give a primed cell a faster or larger response, and this effect should disappear when AP-1 is acutely depleted with an auxin or dTAG degron during the interval. The word 'haploid' points to using single-allele knock-in reporters so the readout is not confounded by copy number.

question: ap1
title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Use an inducible degron tag on c-Jun or c-Fos to remove AP-1 at different stages: during the initial stimulus, during the washout interval, or just before re-stimulation. Then check which stage is needed for the memory signature (chromatin marks, transcriptional priming, and altered response). This shows whether AP-1 is required to maintain the memory or only to write it. The 'hoseless' and 'unreleased' imagery suggests the test of whether the factor must stay bound to keep the state.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-based reporter to track memory in single cells
description: Build an inducible AP-1 activity reporter (such as a FosTRAP-style tamoxifen-dependent recorder or a destabilized-fluorescent Fos-responsive reporter) and follow single cells by live imaging or lineage tracing across divisions. Memory predicts that cells which once had high AP-1 activity keep a heritable, altered response state in their progeny after the signal is gone. The 'tachylalia' idea of rapid, repeated pulses suggests also testing whether pulse frequency, not just total exposure, sets the state.

question: ap1
title: Mathematical model with a falsifiable memory signature
description: Build an ODE or stochastic model of AP-1 feedback (for example, AP-1 inducing its own Fos/Jun expression and chromatin opening) and fit it to the time-course and re-stimulation data. Compare a model with a bistable or hysteretic chromatin switch to one with purely transient signaling, and design a perturbation that the two models predict differently, such as a timed pulse or a partial degradation. This tests whether the data truly need a memory mechanism, which is the strongest way to rule out a transient response that only looks like memory.

question: ap1
title: Washout time course for persistent chromatin marks (bimodal test)
description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus, wash it out, and track AP-1 site accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) at memory loci over days. A memory mechanism predicts that marks persist after stimulus removal and that the population splits into bimodal states rather than decaying smoothly, as a bistable switch would.

question: ap1
title: Degron-based necessity test during the silent interval
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron to deplete FOS or JUN only during the quiescent window after stimulation, then re-challenge and measure whether primed (faster or stronger) transcription of memory genes is lost. This separates AP-1 needed to maintain the memory from AP-1 needed only for the initial response.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic inheritance across cell divisions
description: Induce AP-1 transiently, sort cells by FACS at several generations after washout, and measure chromatin state and re-stimulation responses in daughter cells. Persistence through divisions, especially when AP-1 protein is absent, would indicate heritable self-maintained memory rather than a direct readout of ongoing AP-1 activity.

question: ap1
title: Dose-timing and delay-dependent recall assay
description: Pre-stimulate with varying doses and durations, then re-challenge after increasing delays and fit the decay of the primed response to estimate memory half-life and recall strength. Repeat with DNA-binding-deficient or site-mutant AP-1 at the memory enhancers; a memory mediated by AP-1 should be abolished or shortened in these mutants.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage tracing of heterogeneous memory states
description: Combine a live AP-1 reporter with lineage barcoding and single-cell multiome sequencing to follow individual cells after stimulation, asking whether memory is retained in a subset of cells that shows a hidden, stable chromatin state. Such a state should be predictive of later responses, and its persistence should correlate with AP-1 occupancy at specific enhancers rather than with reporter signal alone.

question: ap1
title: Persistence of AP-1-driven chromatin opening after stimulus washout
description: Pulse cells with a defined stimulus, then wash it out and track FOS/JUN occupancy (CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq) alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac at AP-1 enhancers over days. If AP-1 is a memory mechanism, enhancer accessibility and marks should outlast the decline in AP-1 binding, and the duration should scale with the length of the priming pulse. Chromatin scaffolding is the analogy here: the 'nucleoid-like' state is what carries the record.

question: ap1
title: Primed versus naive re-stimulation kinetics
description: Compare first and second exposures to the same stimulus after a rest period, measuring the timing, amplitude, and recruitment speed of AP-1 binding and target gene transcription (nascent RNA-seq, qPCR time courses). A memory mechanism predicts faster and stronger ('rearoused') responses on re-exposure, and this advantage should disappear when AP-1 binding sites are mutated.

question: ap1
title: Acute, time-resolved depletion of AP-1 during priming versus recall
description: Use a dTAG or auxin degron on endogenous JUN or FOS (or an optogenetic AP-1 switch) to remove AP-1 separately during the priming pulse, during the rest interval, and during the re-stimulation. Memory should be lost only when AP-1 is depleted during the interval or at recall, and not when depletion happens only during priming. This gives a causal test of necessity at each phase, rather than correlation.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage tracking of AP-1 history across divisions
description: Combine a live AP-1 reporter (for example an FOS-destabilized GFP or an AP-1-responsive fluorescent sensor) with time-lapse imaging and lineage barcoding to ask whether a cell's prior AP-1 activity predicts its response to a later stimulus, and whether that predictive value is inherited by daughter cells. Quantifying this heritability (for example with variance decomposition) separates true memory from transient, stimulus-driven variation.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic bookmarking test of AP-1-marked enhancers
description: Sort or image cells in mitosis after priming and measure whether AP-1 and its associated enhancer marks remain on DNA through mitosis (live imaging of tagged JUN, mitotic ChIP-seq). Then check whether daughter cells re-activate target genes faster on the same stimulus. Retention through division is a strong criterion for a stable cellular memory, and loss of bookmarking with preserved memory would argue against AP-1 being the carrier.

question: ap1
title: Stimulus washout and persistence time course
description: Give a brief AP-1-inducing stimulus (e.g., TPA or EGF pulse, or a doxycycline-inducible FOS/JUN pulse), then withdraw it and track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and target transcription over days. Memory requires that AP-1 target enhancers stay open or primed after AP-1 itself has returned to baseline, so persistence beyond the signal is the key readout.

question: ap1
title: Re-stimulation test of primed versus naive cells
description: Compare the first and second responses to the same stimulus, measuring AP-1 target induction, Pol II loading, and enhancer accessibility. Memory predicts faster or stronger re-induction in previously stimulated cells. Pair this with CRISPR mutation of AP-1 motifs at the primed enhancers to test whether the memory depends on those specific sites.

question: ap1
title: Inducible degradation of AP-1 during the memory window
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-based degron on endogenous FOS or JUN to remove AP-1 after priming but before re-stimulation. If AP-1 is the memory carrier, degradation should erase the re-induction advantage while leaving the first-response induction intact. Timing the degradation separately from the priming stimulus separates maintenance of memory from its initial establishment.

question: ap1
title: Coupled AP-1 and histone-mark profiling across time
description: Perform ChIP-seq or CUT&Tag for H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3 alongside AP-1 binding over the same time course. Memory-like behavior would show persistent deposition of activating marks at AP-1-bound enhancers after AP-1 has left them. Comparing these marks with a DNA-methylation or histone-mark-writer knockout shows whether the memory is chromatin-based or relies on AP-1 alone.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 state heritability
description: Combine an AP-1 reporter or live-cell FOS/JUN readout with lineage barcoding so you can follow individual cells through several divisions after a pulse. Quantify how strongly AP-1 activity state in one generation predicts the state in descendants, and whether that correlation disappears when AP-1 is knocked down. Heritable, AP-1-dependent states would indicate cellular memory rather than simple reversible signaling.

question: ap1
title: Post-stimulus persistence of chromatin accessibility (crackled-glaze test)
description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 inducer (e.g., TPA or EGF), then wash out and track AP-1 occupancy (JUN/FOS CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and H3K27ac at AP-1 motifs over days. Memory requires that accessibility and enhancer marks remain after JUN/FOS binding has returned to baseline, like the fine cracks that stay in a crackled glaze after the stress is gone.

question: ap1
title: Acute JUN/FOS degradation after priming
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, then use an auxin-inducible degron to rapidly deplete JUN or FOS before re-stimulation. If primed responses and retained enhancer states survive depletion, the memory is carried by downstream chromatin rather than by continued AP-1 presence; if they vanish, AP-1 itself is required to maintain the memory.

question: ap1
title: Binding-site dependence via dCas9 and motif mutants
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs at endogenous memory-associated enhancers and separately tether dCas9-p300 or dCas9-KRAB to these sites while leaving AP-1 intact. Compare retention of the primed transcriptional response to show whether specific AP-1 binding is necessary and whether writing a chromatin mark is sufficient.

question: ap1
title: Sister-cell lineage tracking of AP-1 activity states
description: Use a live AP-1 transcriptional reporter (destabilized fluorescent protein under an AP-1-responsive enhancer) with time-lapse microscopy to track cell lineages through several divisions. Measure whether prior high or low AP-1 history is heritable across sister cells and predicts later responses to a second stimulus, separating true memory from transient signaling noise.

question: ap1
title: Mitotic bookmarking and memory across cell division
description: Sort mitotic cells from primed and unprimed populations and perform ATAC-seq and AP-1 occupancy assays on mitotic chromatin to see whether AP-1 sites stay accessible during mitosis. Then test whether daughter cells retain the primed state, and whether blocking mitotic bookmarking factors removes the memory.

question: ap1
title: Unmask persistence after AP-1 washout
description: Use an inducible AP-1 system (e.g., 4-OHT-activated FOS-ER or a dTAG-tagged JUN) to pulse AP-1 activity, then remove the inducer and track ATAC-seq, H3K27ac, and AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) at target enhancers over days. If AP-1 is a memory mechanism, chromatin opening and reinduction capacity should persist after AP-1 protein returns to baseline. Analogy: like unmasking a latent signal once the noise has cleared, the stored state should be visible only after the active factor is gone.

question: ap1
title: Degron-timed erasure to separate maintenance from encoding
description: Apply acute AP-1 degradation (dTAG or auxin degron on JUN/FOS) at different times after priming: during induction, during a quiescent interval, and at late timepoints. If AP-1 is required only for encoding, degradation after the interval should not erase the memory, whereas continuous AP-1 requirement for maintenance would show loss of the primed response. Readout is the reinduction of target genes on re-stimulation. Analogy: like unrigging a mechanism at chosen moments to see which parts hold the stored state.

question: ap1
title: Savings assay with motif-mutant enhancers
description: Compare first- and second-exposure transcriptional kinetics (e.g., nascent RNA by TT-seq or smFISH) at endogenous loci, wild-type versus CRISPR-edited TGAGTCA (TRE) motifs in the enhancers. A memory role predicts faster or stronger second responses (savings) that disappear when the AP-1 site is mutated, while non-memory priming would not depend on the motif. question: ap1
title: Lineage-tracked AP-1 reporter for heritable memory
description: Express a destabilized live reporter of AP-1 activity (e.g., FOS promoter-driven d2EGFP) in cells, then track single-cell lineages by time-lapse imaging across several divisions after a transient stimulus. Test whether prior AP-1 activity history predicts the magnitude of future responses in daughter cells, and whether that correlation decays with generation number. Analogy: the way a trait passes through successive generations, like a lineage of cells carrying a state forward.

question: ap1
title: Scrambled-motif and matched-control statistical design
description: Perform JUN/FOS ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN and H3K27ac profiling at matched timepoints after stimulus, comparing AP-1-bound sites to a control set of shuffled or scrambled TRE-like motifs and GC/accessibility-matched random genomic regions. A memory mechanism should show sustained, AP-1-motif-dependent signal at lasting sites that exceeds what generic priming produces at the controls. Analogy: a randomized word list as a null, so that any pattern found must be specific rather than an artifact of composition.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN after transient stimulus

title: Nuclear transplant/relay-race handoff: mitotic inheritance and AP-1 bookmarking
description: Borrowing the baton-pass idea from relay races, ask whether the 'baton' of AP-1 is passed through cell division. Use live imaging of tagged JUN/FOS through mitosis, mitotic-chromosome CUT&RUN, and lineage tracing of sister cells after a pulse, with acute degron depletion (dTAG) of AP-1 members at different cell-cycle phases. Transmission of memory to daughter cells only when AP-1 is present at the handoff would show a bookmarking-based memory mechanism.

question: ap1
title: Magnetic hysteresis loop: dose-response of prior stimulus
description: Borrowing the physics of ferromagnetic hysteresis, expose cells to rising then falling stimulus (e.g., serum/ERK or stress signals) and measure AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target transcription at each step. If the up- and down-sweep curves fail to overlap at equal input, and the loop area depends on AP-1 dosage (via dominant-negative A-FOS), the state is history-dependent, as a memory mechanism requires.

question: ap1
title: Immunological recall assay: primed vs naive re-stimulation
description: Borrowing the vaccine prime-boost design, give a first stimulus, rest cells for days to weeks until FOS/JUN levels return to baseline, then re-stimulate and compare transcriptional kinetics and amplitude with naive cells (RNA-seq, nascent-RNA 4sU-seq). Test causality by acutely degrading AP-1 (dTAG/AID) only during the priming window versus only during the rest period to learn when AP-1 is needed to write versus maintain the memory.

question: ap1
title: Palimpsest/ink-stain analysis: lineage tracing of AP-1-opened enhancers
description: Borrowing from archaeology's palimpsest (traces left after the original writing is erased), use single-cell multiome (scATAC plus RNA) or CUT&Tag after a transient stimulus to identify enhancers that stay accessible and marked (H3K27ac/H3K4me1) after AP-1 leaves. Pair with a lineage barcode to show that these marks are inherited by daughter cells and that their persistence predicts the stronger secondary response in a clone-specific way.

question: ap1
title: Bistable toggle-switch modelling with single-cell live imaging
description: Borrowing from synthetic-biology and dynamical-systems theory of bistable circuits, image endogenous-tagged FOS/JUN and a reporter of target genes live in single cells across pulses of varying duration, then fit ODE models with positive feedback (AP-1 autoregulation at the FOS/JUN promoters). Evidence of memory would be a bimodal distribution, a critical threshold, and hysteresis; model-guided perturbation of the feedback loop (CRISPRi on the AP-1 site in the JUN promoter) should abolish bistability.

question: ap1
title: Molecular 'bookmarking' as in mitotic bookmarking of a library: mitotic chromosome profiling
description: Borrowing the library bookmark idea, test whether AP-1 stays bound to chromatin during mitosis or leaves a pioneer-like footprint by imaging live mitotic cells and by CUT&Tag/ATAC on sorted mitotic cells, then follow reactivation of bookmarked genes in early G1 with or without AP-1 depletion at mitosis. Retention of binding and faster post-mitotic reactivation of bookmarked loci versus non-bookmarked controls would show that AP-1 carries information across cell divisions.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis curves (magnetic-material analogy)
description: Like magnetization hysteresis, expose cells to ramped-up then ramped-down stimulus doses (e.g., optogenetic or chemical activation of the AP-1 upstream kinases JNK/ERK) and measure AP-1 target gene output and chromatin accessibility at matched doses. A loop in which the same dose gives different outputs depending on history indicates bistable, memory-like behavior.

question: ap1
title: Neuronal engram tagging for AP-1 history (immediate-early gene lineage tracing)
description: Borrowing from Fos-TRAP engram labeling, use an AP-1 (Fos/Jun) driven inducible Cre or recorder to permanently mark cells that previously had AP-1 activity. Then re-challenge the marked and unmarked populations after weeks and compare their transcriptional responses by scRNA-seq to see whether past AP-1 activity predicts a faster or stronger response.

question: ap1
title: Pioneer-factor 'trail-marker' footprinting (ecology/animal trail analogy)
description: Perform time-course ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors, BAF subunits, and H3K27ac before stimulation, after it, and after a long washout. Identify enhancers that stay open after AP-1 leaves, as a trail persists after the animal has gone, and test whether AP-1 motif content predicts which loci keep this latent state.

question: ap1
title: Control-theory feedback perturbation (engineering bistable switch test)
description: Model AP-1 positive autoregulation (c-Jun promotes its own transcription) as a feedback circuit with ODEs, and predict the conditions for bistability. Then test it by transiently blocking c-Jun with a degron or dominant-negative (A-Fos) at different times and checking whether the high state persists, collapses, or can be reset, as the model predicts.

question: ap1
title: Immune 'trained immunity' recall assay with causal enhancer editing
description: Using the trained-immunity design, give cells a first stimulus, rest them, then give a second stimulus. Compare cytokine or target gene response with and without AP-1 disruption (CRISPR of AP-1 motifs at specific enhancers, or acute degron of Fos/Jun only during the priming window). If priming-window loss alone abolishes enhanced recall, AP-1 is needed to write the memory rather than only to read it out.

question: ap1
title: Primed vs. virgin hysteresis comparison
description: Pre-stimulate cells (e.g., with EGF, TPA, or a cytokine), withdraw the stimulus for varied rest periods, then restimulate and compare dose-response and induction-kinetics curves of AP-1 target genes against naive cells. Differences in amplitude, threshold, or speed of the second response, plotted as a loop across stimulus history, quantify memory.

question: ap1
title: Chromatin-state mapping of the stored record
description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN/ChIP for FOS/JUN, H3K27ac, and BAF remodeler marks, plus footprinting, in primed, rested, and naive cells to see whether AP-1-bound enhancers remain open after the signal is gone. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motifs that correlates with enhanced re-induction, analogous to imaging dislocation networks, would identify the structural carrier.

question: ap1
title: Annealing-style erasure titration
description: Test how much perturbation is needed to erase memory: dose-titrate inhibitors of chromatin remodeling (BRG1/SWI-SNF), histone acetyltransferases, or DNA replication/cell divisions, and measure when the primed response reverts to naive. If memory decays only with disruption of AP-1-dependent chromatin and not with loss of AP-1 protein levels, the chromatin structure rather than ongoing AP-1 activity carries the record.

question: ap1
title: Acute AP-1 degradation at different time windows
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during priming, during the rest period, or during restimulation, then read out the secondary response. Distinguishing a requirement for writing the memory from maintaining or reading it shows whether AP-1 is the carrier or just an initiator.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell and lineage-tracked history–response mapping
description: Combine live reporters of AP-1 activity (FOS/JUN dynamics) with single-cell RNA/ATAC-seq and lineage tracing across divisions to relate each cell's past AP-1 dynamics to its later response. Heritability of response across sister cells and its decay over generations tests whether memory is cell-intrinsic and stable, as opposed to residual signaling.

question: ap1
title: Ramp-up/ramp-down hysteresis curves of AP-1 target state
description: Titrate a stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or chemically induced c-Fos/c-Jun, or ERK/TPA dose) up and then down in single cells, and measure AP-1 activity and target gene expression at steady state at each dose. A non-overlapping up and down dose-response curve (hysteresis width) shows state-dependent memory, and the width can be compared with AP-1 perturbations (e.g., dominant-negative FOS, JUN phosphomutants).

question: ap1
title: Past-state-predicts-present test with chromatin accessibility proxies
description: After a transient stimulus is withdrawn and current AP-1 and signaling levels are matched to naive controls, use ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag for AP-1 binding and accessibility at enhancers to test whether prior exposure still predicts accessibility and transcriptional output. Use this like a proxy record: regress the response on history after controlling for present conditions, and ask whether AP-1 motif-containing sites hold the residual.

question: ap1
title: Autocorrelation and critical-slowing-down analysis of live AP-1 reporters
description: Image single-cell AP-1 reporter or endogenously tagged FOS/JUN dynamics over days and compute autocorrelation time, variance and relaxation rates after small perturbations at different stimulus doses. Rising autocorrelation and variance near a threshold, plus long relaxation times, indicate bistability or slow feedback, and the memory timescale is estimated directly.

question: ap1
title: Memory-decay timescale mapping via re-stimulation after variable rest
description: Give a priming pulse, wait for varied intervals (minutes to weeks, across cell divisions), then give a second test pulse and measure the change in response amplitude and kinetics. Fitting the decay of primed-versus-naive response difference gives the memory timescale, and comparing it with AP-1 level, binding and chromatin marks tests whether AP-1 is required for persistence.

question: ap1
title: Perturb-the-memory-carrier with model-based forcing experiments
description: Build a dynamical model (positive feedback via FOS/JUN autoinduction and chromatin) fit to the ramp and relaxation data, then use it to predict thresholds. Test it by acutely degrading AP-1 (degron, CRISPRi) at different times after priming: if the memory is carried by AP-1, loss after priming should erase the primed response, whereas if chromatin carries it, the response should persist and could be restored when AP-1 is returned.

question: ap1
title: Persistence-after-withdrawal test (washout time course)
description: Give a transient stimulus (e.g., EGF, TPA, or injury signal), then remove it and track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN) and target gene expression over days of washout. Memory is indicated if accessibility and transcriptional priming persist well beyond AP-1 activity returning to baseline, analogous to testing for effects that persist after the incentive is removed.

question: ap1
title: Cohort-style timing design with re-stimulation (primed vs naive)
description: Compare cells exposed at different times or doses (early vs late, single vs repeated) against never-exposed matched controls, then challenge all with the same second stimulus. Use a difference-in-differences model on the response (gene induction, enhancer opening) to estimate the exposure-history effect, controlling for current AP-1 levels, much as cohort comparisons isolate imprinting from current incentives.

question: ap1
title: Lagged-term regression on single-cell multiome data
description: In single-cell RNA plus ATAC time series, regress the current state of target loci on both current AP-1 (FOS/JUN) activity and lagged AP-1 activity or past accessibility. A significant lagged coefficient after conditioning on present AP-1 supports memory, while dependence only on current levels supports ongoing incentive-driven regulation.

question: ap1
title: Acute degradation of AP-1 after the exposure (removing the current incentive)
description: Use degron-tagged JUN/FOS (dTAG or auxin-inducible) or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS. Degrade AP-1 only after the priming stimulus, then test whether accessibility and enhanced re-induction persist. Compare with degradation before or during priming to separate the role of AP-1 in establishing memory from its role in maintaining it.

question: ap1
title: Natural-experiment-like quasi-random exposure via heterogeneity or optogenetics
description: Use optogenetic or chemogenetic control of AP-1 pulses (such as light-inducible FOS/JUN) so that exposure history is assigned randomly across cells or wells, independent of cell state. Measure later chromatin and transcriptional outcomes as a function of pulse number, duration and timing, which gives causal dose-history relationships free of the selection confounds in endogenous exposure.

question: ap1
title: Write-remove-read retention assay for AP-1 chromatin state
description: Apply a transient stimulus (e.g., a defined pulse of TPA, a growth factor, or optogenetic c-Fos/c-Jun activation), then wash it out. Track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene expression at timepoints from hours to many cell divisions. Retention is shown if accessibility and output persist after AP-1 activity itself has decayed to baseline.

question: ap1
title: Dose-sweep hysteresis mapping of AP-1 targets
description: Ramp stimulus intensity up and then down in separate cell populations. Use single-cell readouts such as a reporter or scRNA-seq for AP-1 target output at each step. If the up and down response curves differ, with bimodal populations at intermediate doses, the system has hysteresis and bistability, which are signatures of memory rather than simple tracking of input.

question: ap1
title: Read-out test: does the stored state change later responses?
description: After a priming pulse and washout, challenge primed and naive cells with a second stimulus. Compare the speed, amplitude and gene set of the response, including whether it needs AP-1 or only chromatin accessibility. This checks that the retained state causally changes output, as a memory element's stored value must when it is read.

question: ap1
title: Erase and rewrite perturbations with degron and dominant-negative AP-1
description: Add a degron or dominant-negative (e.g., A-Fos) at different times: during priming, only after washout, or at the time of the second challenge. If removing AP-1 after priming erases the memory, AP-1 is needed to maintain it. If removal only during priming blocks it, AP-1 is needed only to write it, and the memory is held elsewhere (e.g., histone marks or other TFs). Test whether re-pulsing resets the state.

question: ap1
title: Stress-testing durability with cycling, noise and division
description: Subject primed cells to repeated stimulation cycles, signaling noise (kinase inhibitor, fluctuating ligand), temperature or metabolic stress, and many cell divisions. Use live-cell AP-1 reporters in lineage-tracked single cells to measure how long the state lasts, how often it flips, and whether it is inherited by daughter cells. Fit a stochastic switching model to estimate memory half-life and robustness.

question: ap1
title: Apparent-time chromatin comparison after stimulus removal
description: Like comparing older and younger speakers without ongoing exposure, stimulate cells (e.g., with serum, TPA, or injury signals), then withdraw the stimulus and profile AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, ATAC-seq accessibility and H3K27ac at multiple 'generations' (days and cell divisions) post-withdrawal. Persistence of AP-1-motif-linked accessible sites in the absence of the stimulus and of AP-1 re-expression indicates memory rather than ongoing signaling.

question: ap1
title: Cognate-set comparison of AP-1 sites across cell states and lineages
description: Treat AP-1-bound enhancers as 'cognate sets' and compare them across primed, naive, and descendant cells to classify sites as inherited (retained through divisions and differentiation) versus newly acquired (de novo from current signaling). Use motif grammar and conservation to distinguish stable memory sites from transient ones.

question: ap1
title: Phylogenetic lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Use barcoded lineage tracing with single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) to build clonal trees and test whether AP-1 accessibility and target-gene expression states are shared among sister cells beyond what the current environment predicts. Phylogenetic-signal statistics (e.g., Pagel's lambda or heritability along the tree) separate heritable memory from convergent responses to shared signals.

question: ap1
title: Acoustic-style quantitative dose-response of re-stimulation
description: Measure the kinetics and amplitude of transcription (nascent RNA-seq, live reporters) in primed versus naive cells upon second stimulation, as phonetic measures quantify subtle residual features. Faster or stronger induction of AP-1 targets in primed cells, quantified across priming doses and rest intervals, gives a memory signature with a measurable decay time.

question: ap1
title: Substrate-removal causal perturbation
description: Test whether the memory outlasts its originating influence by acutely degrading or knocking out AP-1 (dTAG/AID degron, dominant-negative A-FOS) after priming. Then check whether accessibility and enhanced re-response persist, and whether re-expression is needed to re-open sites. This distinguishes AP-1 as initiator versus maintainer of memory, with other factors carrying it forward.

question: ap1
title: Chronology of AP-1 binding and chromatin opening (geochronology analogue)
description: After a defined stimulus (e.g., serum, TPA, injury, or inflammatory cue), run time-resolved ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN family members, and H3K27ac at many time points through and long after signal withdrawal. Date which AP-1-bound enhancers stay open or primed, and for how long, to establish whether a persistent 'record' exists and how it decays.

question: ap1
title: Stratigraphic reading of the preserved signal on chromatin
description: Use single-cell multiome (scATAC plus RNA) and footprinting or motif-deviation analysis of sequential stimulation histories, such as stimulus A then B, to read layered AP-1 imprints. Test whether sites opened by the first stimulus (AP-1-dependent 'sediment layers') are distinguishable from sites opened by the second, and whether the AP-1 subunit composition (FOS vs JUN vs ATF) encodes the identity of the earlier event.

question: ap1
title: Naive versus pre-exposed 'flume' response test
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, wash out, rest them, then challenge with the same or a different stimulus. Compare transcription kinetics (nascent RNA, PRO-seq) and amplitude against naive cells, and test whether the faster or stronger response at primed loci depends on the prior AP-1 occupancy. This is the direct analogue of testing whether a landscape with prior history erodes differently.

question: ap1
title: Perturbing the record: acute AP-1 degradation at different times
description: Use degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) tools to remove AP-1 either during the priming event, during the rest period, or only at the challenge. If memory needs AP-1 only at writing, only at maintenance, or only at reading, the timing separates writing, storage and readout roles. Pair with CRISPR mutation of specific AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers to test sufficiency and necessity at individual loci.

question: ap1
title: Numerical modeling of memory dynamics and lineage tracing across divisions
description: Fit a mathematical model (bistable or hysteretic feedback, including AP-1 positive autoregulation of JUN/FOS and chromatin-state inertia) to the time-course and dose-response data, and predict memory duration and decay by cell division. Validate by live-cell imaging of AP-1 reporters or fluorescent FOS and by sister-cell or lineage tracking, testing whether the state is inherited through mitosis, with mitotic bookmarking assays (imaging and CUT&RUN on mitotic cells).

question: ap1
title: Regression-discontinuity around the old stimulus boundary
description: Expose cells to graded doses or durations of an AP-1-inducing stimulus (e.g., serum, TPA, injury, inflammatory cue) and use single-cell imaging or scRNA-seq to compare cells just above versus just below the activation threshold. Test whether a sharp jump in later enhancer accessibility and gene responsiveness appears at the threshold, which would indicate a switch-like memory rather than a smooth dose-response.

question: ap1
title: Historical-legacy time-course linking past AP-1 occupancy to present responses
description: Do longitudinal ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN, and H3K27ac in the same cell lineage before, during, and long after transient stimulation, after AP-1 levels return to baseline. Regress the strength of the secondary response on prior AP-1 binding at each enhancer, to test whether sites that were occupied earlier remain accessible and more responsive after the original input is gone.

question: ap1
title: Instrumental-variable style causal perturbation with acute degradation
description: Use a dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS) or a degron-tagged JUN/FOS to remove AP-1 either only during the initial stimulus or only during the later restimulation. If memory requires AP-1 only at the encoding stage, or also at maintenance and recall, the two windows should dissociate. This separates AP-1 as a causal carrier of memory from correlated factors such as chromatin remodelers or other TFs.

question: ap1
title: Placebo sites and placebo stimuli
description: Compare AP-1 motif-containing loci that were never bound with those that were, and compare cells given an unrelated stimulus (e.g., a different signaling pathway) with AP-1-stimulated cells. Add motif-mutation or CRISPR-edited enhancer controls so that any retained accessibility or priming is shown to be specific to prior AP-1 binding and not to general stress or cell-state changes.

question: ap1
title: Process tracing of the transmission mechanism across divisions
description: Track lineages with live reporters or barcoded clones to measure whether the primed state persists through cell divisions and decays at a defined rate. Pair this with perturbations of candidate carriers (BAF/SWI-SNF recruitment, pioneer cofactors, histone marks, mitotic bookmarking of AP-1) to find which mechanism transmits the memory, and fit a quantitative model to heritability versus decay.

question: ap1
title: Acute degradation/inhibition of AP-1 after the stimulus (causal ablation of the 'hidden state')
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus (e.g., serum, TNF, or injury signal), then after the stimulus is removed, use degron-tagged FOS/JUN or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) to acutely deplete AP-1 at defined delays, and measure whether the enhanced response to a second stimulus is lost. If memory requires AP-1 during the retention window, and not only during priming, this separates maintenance from encoding.

question: ap1
title: Patching AP-1 binding sites in chromatin (site-specific intervention)
description: Use dCas9-based tools or motif mutation by base editing to block or remove AP-1 motifs at specific enhancers that gained accessibility after priming, then test whether re-stimulation transcription at the linked genes is selectively reduced. This is analogous to patching individual units: it tests whether specific AP-1-marked loci causally carry the memory for particular downstream genes.

question: ap1
title: Linear-probe-style decoding of past stimulus history from AP-1 state
description: Collect single-cell multiome data (ATAC with AP-1 motif accessibility/ChromVAR, FOS/JUN levels) from cells with different prior stimulus histories (type, dose, duration), and train classifiers to decode that history from AP-1 features alone after a washout. Compare decoding from AP-1 features with that from other TFs or random features to show AP-1 specifically stores the information.

question: ap1
title: Delay and distractor retention-timescale experiments
description: Vary the washout interval between prime and challenge (hours to weeks, across cell divisions) and insert distractor stimuli (an unrelated pathway activator) in between, while tracking AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN/ChIP) and the secondary response magnitude. The decay curve of AP-1 binding and response, and its robustness to distractors, defines the memory timescale and whether it survives division.

question: ap1
title: Live-cell reporters with sufficiency tests via state transplantation
description: Image endogenous-tagged FOS/JUN dynamics and an AP-1 target reporter in single cells with lineage tracking, testing whether past AP-1 activity levels predict later responses in the same cell and in daughters. Then optogenetically or chemically drive AP-1 in naive cells (without the original stimulus) to test whether AP-1 activity alone is sufficient to install the primed, persistent response, like writing a state into a hidden vector and seeing if it changes outputs.

question: ap1
title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-and-chase
description: Use light-inducible FOS/JUN (or optogenetic dimerization) to deliver precisely defined AP-1 activity pulses in the absence of any upstream signal, then measure whether a transient pulse alone leaves a lasting transcriptional/accessibility state and how its duration depends on pulse dose and frequency. This separates AP-1 sufficiency from upstream signaling.

question: ap1
title: Acute degron removal after priming (necessity for maintenance vs. establishment)
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN family members with dTAG/auxin degrons and deplete them either only during priming, only after priming (during the memory interval), or only at recall. If memory requires AP-1 to persist, post-priming depletion should erase it, whereas establishment-only requirement indicates AP-1 acts as an initiator of another memory carrier.

question: ap1
title: Live-cell single-cell AP-1 reporter lineage tracking
description: Track endogenous AP-1 activity (knock-in fluorescent FOS/JUN or a synthetic TRE reporter) in individual cells and their daughters through division using time-lapse microscopy, then correlate pre-stimulus/ancestral AP-1 history with later response magnitude. Mother-daughter correlation beyond that explained by shared noise would show heritable memory at the single-cell level.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic AP-1 positive-feedback circuit perturbation and mathematical modeling
description: Rewire or break the FOS/JUN autoregulatory loop (e.g., mutate TRE sites in the JUN/FOSL1 promoters, or add a synthetic feedback) and fit dynamical models to dose-response and hysteresis measurements. Observing bistability or hysteresis, which are lost when the loop is cut, would test whether AP-1 network topology itself encodes memory.

question: ap1
title: Targeted motif editing and dCas9 tethering at specific memory enhancers
description: Use base editing to mutate individual AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and conversely tether AP-1 or pioneer-like activation domains with dCas9 at motif-null sites. Measure locus-specific persistence of accessibility, nucleosome remodeling (e.g., SWI/SNF/BAF recruitment), and faster re-induction to establish causal, locus-level sufficiency and necessity.

question: ap1
title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-code memory test
description: Use optogenetically controlled FOS/JUN dimerization or nuclear translocation to deliver defined pulse patterns (duration, frequency, amplitude), then measure whether past pulse history alters later transcriptional output and enhancer opening after a long rest. This separates memory encoded by AP-1 dynamics from memory encoded by upstream signaling.

question: ap1
title: Single-molecule tracking of AP-1 residence on nucleosomal sites over time
description: In live cells, use HaloTag-JUN/FOS single-molecule imaging to compare residence times, bound fraction, and nucleosome engagement at primed versus naive loci or cells, including after stimulus removal. Longer-lived binding or altered search kinetics in primed cells would show a persistent molecular state rather than just a lingering chromatin mark.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-tracing of memory through cell division with barcoded sister cells
description: Split sister cells after priming, then track them with lineage barcodes and paired scRNA/scATAC to test whether AP-1 activity states and primed responses are inherited across divisions and decay at a rate predicted by AP-1 turnover. High sister-cell concordance would indicate heritable memory rather than ongoing signaling.

question: ap1
title: Targeted epigenome editing to uncouple AP-1 sites from memory
description: Use dCas9 tools (for example, dCas9-KRAB or a TET/DNMT module, or a motif-specific CRISPR-based mutation of single AP-1 sites) at selected primed enhancers after priming. Then test whether the recall response requires the AP-1 motif, the local chromatin state, or both. Rescue with synthetic AP-1-independent pioneer recruitment would show whether AP-1 is the memory carrier or just the writer.

question: ap1
title: Mathematical modeling of bistability with perturbation-based fits
description: Build ODE and stochastic models of AP-1 feedback loops (such as FOS/JUN autoregulation and chromatin positive feedback), then test the predicted hysteresis, critical slowing, and bimodal switching by titrating the priming dose and measuring recall in single cells. Agreement between model predictions and observed dose-history dependence would show whether AP-1 network topology can sustain memory.

question: ap1
title: Degron-based temporal separation of establishment vs maintenance
description: Use an acute degron (dTAG/AID) on JUN/FOS family members and degrade them only after priming but before re-challenge. If memory persists without AP-1 protein, it is stored elsewhere. If it collapses, AP-1 is needed for maintenance, not just establishment.

question: ap1
title: Optogenetic/synthetic AP-1 pulse-encoding of memory
description: Drive AP-1 with a light-inducible FOS/JUN or a synthetic AP-1 transactivator using defined pulse durations and frequencies, without the upstream stimulus. Then measure target-gene response to a later challenge to see whether AP-1 activity alone is sufficient to write memory, and how its dose and dynamics set memory strength.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage-tracked memory inheritance through division
description: Combine live imaging of an AP-1 reporter and a target-gene reporter with lineage tracking across several divisions after a transient stimulus. Then compute mother-daughter and sister-cell correlations and decay half-life, to test whether the memory state is mitotically heritable and clonal rather than a transient signaling echo.

question: ap1
title: Targeted motif editing and synthetic AP-1 site insertion
description: Use base editing to mutate specific AP-1 motifs at a memory-associated enhancer, and insert AP-1 sites at a non-memory locus. Measure whether the locus gains or loses primed accessibility and a faster re-induction, to test cis-level necessity and sufficiency.

question: ap1
title: Single-molecule footprinting of residence and nucleosome occupancy
description: Apply single-molecule footprinting (e.g., Fiber-seq or SMF) and live single-molecule tracking of JUN/FOS before and after stimulus washout. Read out whether individual enhancer molecules stay nucleosome-free or bound, and measure AP-1 residence times. This distinguishes a stable remodeled state from continuous AP-1 occupancy, and from a bistable or hysteretic switch.

question: ap1
title: Optogenetic/degron pulse-chase of AP-1 timing
description: Use an optogenetically controlled or auxin-degron c-Jun/Fos to deliver defined activity pulses and to remove AP-1 at set times after priming (not only during it). If memory persists after degradation, AP-1 only initiates it. If memory decays when AP-1 is removed, AP-1 maintains it.

question: ap1
title: Single-molecule live imaging of residence time and re-binding
description: Track endogenously HaloTagged Fos/Jun by single-molecule tracking at defined loci (e.g., with a CRISPR-based locus label) in primed and naive cells. Test whether priming changes residence time, search kinetics, or the fraction of bound molecules, and whether the changes persist after AP-1 levels return to baseline.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic AP-1 site editing and dCas9 recruitment at one enhancer
description: Mutate or insert AP-1 motifs at a single memory-associated enhancer, or tether dCas9–Fos/Jun or dCas9–repressor to it. Test whether this locus alone is necessary and sufficient to give primed accessibility and a faster re-response, which separates causal local memory from global effects.

question: ap1
title: Pioneer-factor cooperation and nucleosome positioning test
description: Compare MNase-seq/nucleosome maps and BAF (SWI/SNF) occupancy at AP-1 sites after priming. Acute BRG1 inhibition or degradation after priming would test whether AP-1-dependent remodeling is what holds sites open, and whether other factors such as CEBP, ETS or glucocorticoid receptor are needed to maintain memory.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-tracing of memory through cell division with 3D genome readout
description: Prime cells, track their lineages for several divisions by barcoding or live-cell tracking, and test response in descendants. Pair this with Micro-C or HiChIP at AP-1 enhancer–promoter loops, and use mitotic bookmarking assays on mitotic chromosomes. Together these show whether AP-1-linked states are inherited and whether they depend on retained AP-1 or on a copied chromatin state.

question: ap1
title: Acute degron depletion after priming (temporal separation)
description: Use an auxin/dTAG degron on a pioneer AP-1 member (e.g., FOS/JUN) and deplete it only after the priming stimulus is gone but before recall. Then measure whether enhancer accessibility and the faster recall transcription persist, which separates AP-1 as the maintainer of memory from AP-1 as only the initiator.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic AP-1 site editing at endogenous enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or prime editing to mutate or insert single AP-1 motifs at selected enhancers. Then test whether a motif is necessary and sufficient for stimulus-induced accessibility that persists, and for primed re-induction of the linked gene.

question: ap1
title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-encoding with memory decay kinetics
description: Drive AP-1 with light-controlled FOS/JUN, or with a light-gated activator, using defined pulse durations, amplitudes and frequencies. Then measure how long the primed state lasts and how it scales with dose. Bistability, hysteresis, or a threshold would point to a self-sustaining memory circuit. Simple decay would not.

question: ap1
title: Lineage-tracked memory inheritance through division
description: Barcode or live-image single cells, let them divide after priming, and sort sister cells. Measure AP-1 activity (reporter) and accessibility/recall response in the sisters and in later generations, and compare sister concordance with that of random pairs. High concordance that lasts for many divisions, in cells with no ongoing stimulus, would indicate heritable memory.

question: ap1
title: Nucleosome and cofactor handoff profiling (BAF, p300, mitotic bookmarking)
description: Run CUT&Tag for AP-1, SWI/SNF (BRG1/ARID1A) and p300, plus MNase or single-molecule footprinting, in interphase and mitotically arrested primed cells. Test whether AP-1 stays on the DNA through mitosis (bookmarking) or whether it hands off to other factors that keep the sites open. Then perturb the handoff partner to see which one carries the memory.

question: ap1
title: Optogenetic/chemogenetic AP-1 pulse-sufficiency test
description: Use a light- or drug-inducible FOS/JUN (or degron-controlled) to deliver a defined transient AP-1 pulse in the absence of any natural stimulus, then test whether the cells show durable enhancer opening and enhanced responses to a later, unrelated cue. This separates sufficiency of AP-1 for imprinting from correlative occupancy.

question: ap1
title: Time-resolved degron: priming-only vs recall-only depletion
description: Use an acute auxin/dTAG degron on endogenous AP-1 factors and deplete them either only during the priming window, only during the maintenance interval, or only at recall. Memory requiring AP-1 for establishment but not maintenance, or for both, distinguishes a trigger from a self-sustaining memory mechanism.

question: ap1
title: Pioneer-factor-independent maintenance via synthetic enhancer reporters
description: Integrate matched reporter constructs with wild-type, mutated, or spacing-altered AP-1 motifs (plus neighbors like ETS/CEBP) at a fixed genomic safe-harbor locus, and measure whether they acquire and keep a primed state after transient stimulation. This tests whether AP-1 motifs are sufficient in cis to encode memory independent of the native context.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage-tracked inheritance across divisions
description: Label sister cells with barcodes or time-lapse lineage tracing, with an endogenous AP-1 reporter, and compare memory strength (recall response) among sisters and cousins over several divisions. Heritable correlation beyond what is explained by AP-1 levels would indicate mitotic transmission, and mitotic-chromatin imaging or CUT&Tag of mitotic cells would test bookmarking.

question: ap1
title: Single-molecule dynamics and nucleosome-remodeler dependence
description: Perform live-cell single-molecule tracking of Fos/Jun residence times at primed versus naive enhancers, and combine with inhibition/degradation of SWI/SNF (BAF) to test if sustained accessibility needs continual AP-1–BAF recruitment. Long residence or BAF dependence would indicate a mechanistic basis for memory, versus a passive epigenetic scar.

question: ap1
title: Acute degron rescue-timing experiment
description: Use an auxin/dTAG degron on endogenous JUN/FOS family members and deplete AP-1 only during the maintenance phase (after the priming stimulus is gone) versus only during priming. If memory needs AP-1 only for establishment and not maintenance, it is not a self-sustaining memory mechanism. Persistent dependence would support it.

question: ap1
title: Motif-mutated enhancer knock-in with epigenetic readout
description: Use CRISPR base editing to mutate single AP-1 sites at memory-associated enhancers. Then test whether primed accessibility, nearby H3K27ac, and faster re-induction of the target gene are lost. This shows the sites themselves are needed at specific loci, which is stronger than global AP-1 loss.

question: ap1
title: Pioneer-like trapping via single-molecule residence imaging
description: Use live-cell single-molecule tracking of Halo-tagged FOS/JUN, with FRAP, in naive versus primed nuclei. Test whether residence time or bound fraction stays elevated at primed loci for days after the stimulus. This distinguishes lasting engagement from reactivation of binding.

question: ap1
title: Heritability through mitosis with lineage tracing
description: Sort or live-image primed cells and follow daughter cells across several divisions, using an AP-1 reporter and a target-gene reporter. Add mitotic-bookmarking assays such as CUT&Tag on mitotic-arrested cells. Quantify how memory decays over divisions and whether AP-1 bookmarking predicts which lineages retain memory.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic AP-1 pulse-sufficiency test with optogenetics
description: Drive AP-1 activity with an optogenetic or chemogenetic FOS/JUN system, with no upstream signal, using varied pulse patterns (single, repeated, sustained). Measure whether this alone leaves lasting accessibility and a primed transcriptional response, and map the dose–duration threshold for memory. This tests sufficiency and the dynamics needed, instead of only necessity.

question: ap1
title: Optogenetic/chemogenic pulse-timing of AP-1 with a memory-persistence readout
description: Use light- or ligand-inducible FOS/JUN (or degron-controlled) to deliver defined pulses of AP-1 activity in AP-1-null cells, then measure whether enhancer accessibility and a reporter response persist after AP-1 is removed. Varying pulse duration, frequency, and the delay before re-challenge defines the sufficiency, dose-dependence, and decay kinetics of memory.

question: ap1
title: Acute degron depletion after priming (separating establishment from maintenance)
description: Prime cells, then rapidly degrade endogenous AP-1 (dTAG/AID on FOS/JUN/FOSL family members) only during the rest period and not during recall. If the memory persists without AP-1, it is an initiator rather than a maintainer, whereas loss of memory indicates continuous AP-1 requirement. Pair this with nascent-transcript and accessibility readouts.

question: ap1
title: Pioneer-factor residence and nucleosome-positioning footprinting by single-molecule methods
description: Use Fiber-seq or single-molecule footprinting (SMF) on primed vs naive cells to determine, on individual DNA molecules, whether AP-1 sites remain nucleosome-free or bound after signal decay. Live-cell single-molecule tracking of HaloTag-FOS/JUN could also show whether residence time or binding fraction differs in primed cells.

question: ap1
title: Cell-lineage tracing with a lineage-barcoded split-population memory test
description: Use barcoded cells to split sibling clones before and after priming, then track across divisions to see whether the primed state is inherited by daughters and how many divisions it persists. Comparing clonal concordance of recall responses to that of non-sibling cells quantifies mitotic heritability, and AP-1 perturbation in one sibling set tests its role.

question: ap1
title: Targeted epigenome editing of AP-1 sites to test locus-specific causality
description: Use dCas9-based tools (e.g., KRAB, TET1, or DNMT3A) or base-editing of AP-1 motifs at selected enhancers in primed cells, then test locus-specific recall of the response. Conversely, tethering AP-1 domains with dCas9 at a naive locus tests whether local AP-1 recruitment alone is sufficient to install heritable accessibility and faster reactivation.

question: ap1
title: Washout time course with acute degron depletion
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, then after washout acutely degrade JUN/FOS (dTAG/AID) at different delays, measuring retention of chromatin accessibility (ATAC) and transcriptional responsiveness. If accessibility persists without AP-1, it was only needed for establishment; if it collapses, AP-1 actively maintains memory.

question: ap1
title: Priming and re-stimulation hysteresis assay
description: Vary the number, duration, and spacing of stimulus pulses and measure the magnitude and kinetics of the second response (nascent RNA, e.g., PRO-seq) in primed versus naive cells. Test whether the enhanced response depends on AP-1 using A-FOS expressed only during priming versus only during recall.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage-traced multiome
description: Use barcoded clones or sister-cell pairing with joint scRNA/scATAC to test whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression states are shared among related cells beyond what is expected by chance after stimulus removal. Compare concordance across divisions to quantify heritability and its decay.

question: ap1
title: Live imaging of endogenous AP-1 reporters across divisions
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN and a target-gene reporter, then track mother-daughter lineages by time-lapse to see whether activity states persist through mitosis and across generations. Pair with mitotic CUT&RUN to test whether AP-1 bookmarks chromatin.

question: ap1
title: Motif editing and dCas9 tethering at memory enhancers
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers to test necessity for persistent accessibility and faster recall, and conversely tether AP-1 or its pioneer domain via dCas9 to naive loci to test sufficiency to establish a heritable open state. Read out with ATAC, H3K27ac and reporter expression over weeks.

question: ap1
title: Washout time-course of AP-1 occupancy and accessibility
description: After a transient stimulus, profile FOS/JUN CUT&RUN and ATAC footprinting at multiple times post-washout to see whether AP-1 binding and open chromatin persist beyond signaling and TF protein levels. Persistent sites that predict faster secondary transcription define candidate memory loci.

question: ap1
title: Stage-specific acute degradation (degron) of AP-1
description: Use dTAG/AID-tagged JUN/FOS to deplete AP-1 only during priming, only during the memory (washout) interval, or only at rechallenge, then measure the secondary response. This separates AP-1 as the initiator from AP-1 as the maintainer of memory.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell multiome with lineage/sister-cell tracking
description: Combine live imaging of endogenously tagged FOS/JUN with sister-cell tracking and post-hoc multiome to test whether AP-1 state and accessibility are inherited across divisions and predict each cell's re-response. Mitotic retention can be checked simultaneously.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis and optogenetic dose-duration mapping
description: Drive AP-1 with optogenetic or titratable inputs across ramp-up and ramp-down sweeps and varied pulse patterns, then measure output. Path-dependent output (hysteresis) or persistent state would indicate feedback-based memory.

question: ap1
title: Locus-specific motif editing and dCas9 perturbation
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers, or recruit AP-1 or dominant-negative A-FOS with dCas9, and test primed re-response by RNA and accessibility. Loss or gain of memory at single loci tests necessity and sufficiency independent of global AP-1 changes.

question: ap1
title: Stimulus-withdrawal degron separation of priming and recall
description: Endogenously tag FOS/JUN (or use A-FOS) with a degron, deplete AP-1 only during priming, only after washout, or only at restimulation, and measure the recall transcriptional response. This tests whether AP-1 is needed to establish memory, to maintain it, or only to read it out.

question: ap1
title: Longitudinal AP-1 occupancy versus accessibility after washout
description: Run CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac at multiple time points after a transient stimulus to identify sites that stay open after AP-1 leaves. Persistence of accessibility without AP-1 would point to AP-1 acting as an initiator, with the memory held in chromatin state.

question: ap1
title: Motif-mutation of memory enhancers by CRISPR
description: Use base editing or CRISPR to disrupt AP-1 motifs at a few enhancers that show primed accessibility and faster re-induction, then test for loss of the memory effect. This gives causal, locus-specific evidence that AP-1 binding encodes the memory.

question: ap1
title: Optogenetic AP-1 dose and frequency titration with challenge response
description: Use light-controlled AP-1 activation with defined pulse numbers, durations, and intervals, then give a standard second challenge. Memory strength as a function of pulse pattern and decay interval would show whether AP-1 integrates history, and over what timescale.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell multiome with lineage tracking across divisions
description: Perform single-cell RNA+ATAC on primed versus naive cells over several divisions, using barcodes or sister-cell pairing, to link AP-1 motif accessibility to recall strength. Matched sister-cell behavior would show whether the memory is heritable and AP-1-dependent.

question: ap1
title: Timed degron depletion to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, then acutely degrade FOS/JUN (dTAG/AID) at different times after washout, before restimulation. If memory (faster or stronger transcription, retained accessibility) is lost upon late depletion, AP-1 is needed to maintain it, not only to set it up.

question: ap1
title: Pulse-pattern optogenetic AP-1 activation with memory readout
description: Use optogenetic or chemically gated AP-1 to deliver defined pulse numbers, durations and intervals, then test the response to a later challenge. Dependence on pulse history and a decay time constant would show AP-1 activity itself encodes memory, independent of upstream signaling.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage-resolved tracking across divisions
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN together with a target-enhancer reporter, and follow sister cells through division after priming. Heritable differences in response, together with AP-1 mitotic retention, would test whether memory is carried by AP-1 or by downstream chromatin.

question: ap1
title: Motif-level CRISPR editing plus synthetic AP-1 recruitment
description: Delete or mutate AP-1 motifs at specific memory enhancers and ask if priming is lost. Conversely, recruit AP-1 to a neutral locus with dCas9 and ask if it creates a persistent, restimulation-competent state. This tests necessity and sufficiency at the locus level.

question: ap1
title: Hysteresis and bistability of the FOS/JUN feedback circuit
description: Measure single-cell dose-response with increasing versus decreasing stimulus, and perturb the FOS/JUN autoregulatory loop while fitting a mathematical model. Bimodality and hysteresis dependent on the loop would support a self-sustaining circuit memory that does not need a chromatin mark.

question: ap1
title: Timed degron depletion: establishment vs. maintenance
description: Use dTAG/AID-tagged FOS/JUN family members and deplete during the first stimulus only, or only after stimulus withdrawal but before rechallenge. Measuring recall transcription and accessibility distinguishes AP-1 as an initiator from AP-1 as a continuously required maintainer of memory.

question: ap1
title: Long-chase occupancy and accessibility time course
description: Perform CUT&RUN for AP-1 subunits and ATAC-seq at multiple times after transient stimulus, extending through many cell divisions. Test whether AP-1-bound, newly opened sites persist after AP-1 levels return to baseline, and whether persistence predicts stronger rechallenge response.

question: ap1
title: Sufficiency by synthetic AP-1 recruitment
description: Use optogenetic or chemically induced AP-1 activation, or dCas9-targeted AP-1 domains, at specific loci in naive cells with a pulse and then withdrawal. If the locus retains accessibility and shows primed re-induction without the native stimulus, AP-1 is sufficient for memory.

question: ap1
title: Motif-level necessity at memory enhancers
description: Use base editing or CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at selected memory-associated enhancers, then run a stimulus-rest-rechallenge paradigm. Compare chromatin marks and gene induction with unedited controls and with edits to neighboring non-AP-1 motifs to establish cis-level necessity.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell lineage-resolved memory and mitotic bookmarking
description: Combine live-cell FOS/JUN reporters or barcoded lineage tracing with single-cell multiome readouts, and image or profile AP-1 on mitotic chromatin. Test whether sister cells share memory states and AP-1 occupancy, and whether blocking division or bookmarking alters inheritance.

question: ap1
title: Post-stimulus degron depletion
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, then acutely degrade FOS/JUN (dTAG/AID) after the stimulus ends and before re-challenge. If the faster or stronger secondary response is lost, AP-1 is needed to maintain memory and not only to establish it.

question: ap1
title: Chromatin state tracking through washout
description: Run CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN and ATAC-seq plus H3K27ac at several times after stimulus removal. Compare how long AP-1 occupancy, accessibility and marks persist, and whether accessibility outlasts AP-1 binding, which would indicate AP-1 acts as an initiator and not a maintainer.

question: ap1
title: Single-cell hysteresis imaging
description: Image an endogenous FOS or AP-1 reporter in single cells through repeated stimulus pulses with variable intervals. Look for history-dependent responses and heritable states across divisions, and link them to later transcription by lineage tracking.

question: ap1
title: Motif-specific enhancer editing
description: Use CRISPR base or prime editing to mutate AP-1 motifs at selected primed enhancers, then compare the secondary response with unedited controls. This tests whether AP-1 binding at those specific sites is required for the memory at the associated genes.

question: ap1
title: Synthetic AP-1 recruitment sufficiency test
